whyCorrect: The hazard is that hydrogen burns readily in air, and hydrogen is the lifting gas itself, not an optional extra. A designer can manage a hazard built into the material, but cannot get rid of it while still using that gas, so the blank has to mean remove completely. Eliminate is the only choice that names removal, and the word entirely in front of it fits it exactly.

whyWrong.B: Measure describes quantifying the risk, which designers could in fact do; the sentence needs something they could not do.
whyWrong.C: Welcome would mean they were glad of the fire risk, which contradicts weighing it as a hazard.
whyWrong.D: Postpone treats the fire risk as an event that could be delayed, but the danger is present the whole time hydrogen is in the hull.

tips: When the blank follows could not entirely, look for a word that means total removal rather than partial management.

whyCorrect: The first sentence sets the standard: one dust speck ruins every circuit it touches. The measures listed next go far beyond normal cleaning, and the last sentence concedes they look extravagant but explains why they are needed. The blank therefore has to say that normal cleanliness falls short of what the dimensions demand, which is what inadequate says.

whyWrong.B: Expensive describes cost, but the contrast in the sentence is between what looks excessive and what the scale actually requires.
whyWrong.C: Unavailable would mean ordinary cleanliness cannot be obtained, when the point is that it can be obtained and still is not enough.
whyWrong.D: Customary means usual, which is true of ordinary cleanliness by definition and so explains nothing about why the extra measures are justified.

commonMistakes: Choosing a word that is true of ordinary cleanliness rather than one that explains the contrast the sentence sets up.

whyCorrect: The structure is looks _____ until a cornice has had to be cut twice, so the blank names how the distinction seems to someone who has not yet paid for ignoring it, and the until clause overturns that impression. Insisting on the bed rather than the quarry sounds like fussing over a trivial label. Pedantic names exactly that impression of excessive attention to fine distinctions, and the ruined cornice shows the distinction was substantive after all.

whyWrong.A: Profitable would not be overturned by the cost of recutting; the until clause has to reverse the impression, not confirm it.
whyWrong.B: Obligatory says the distinction was required, which the recut cornice would support rather than correct.
whyWrong.C: Traditional makes the practice a matter of custom, but the passage grounds it in how the stone behaves under a chisel.

tips: With looks X until Y, pick the word Y disproves — the sentence is built to reverse the first impression.

whyCorrect: Mansa Musa poured an enormous quantity of gold into Cairo's markets, and flooding a market with any commodity drives its price down. The word still signals that the effect persisted more than a decade later, so the blank has to describe a lasting condition, not a moment. Depressed names a price pushed below its normal level and held there, which is why the chroniclers recorded the episode with irritation.

whyWrong.A: Fixed says the price stopped moving, but nothing in the passage sets a price or freezes it; the point is the direction it moved.
whyWrong.C: Climbing reverses the economics — adding a large supply of gold to a market lowers its price rather than raising it.
whyWrong.D: Unrecorded contradicts the sentence itself, which says Egyptian chroniclers recorded the detail.

commonMistakes: Assuming that because Musa was spectacularly wealthy the price of gold must have risen; supply going up pushes price down.

whyCorrect: The passage explains that the bay's natural period of oscillation nearly matches the period of the tide, so each new tide arrives in step with the water already moving. Two motions arriving in step add together, and the result the passage is explaining is a tide far larger than the one outside. Reinforce is the word for waves that add, and it is the only choice that accounts for the sixteen-metre range.

whyWrong.A: Cancel is what happens when motions arrive out of step, which would make the tide smaller rather than the largest on the coast.
whyWrong.B: Resemble states a similarity between the two motions but describes no interaction, so it cannot explain the extra height.
whyWrong.C: Displace suggests one motion pushes the other aside, which would replace the existing sloshing rather than build on it.

tips: In step is the giveaway for resonance: aligned waves add, opposed waves cancel.

whyCorrect: The text opens by naming what a vacuum tube needs in order to amplify — a stream of electrons crossing an evacuated space, released by a heated filament. It then describes the 1947 germanium experiment and stresses that nothing was heated and nothing was evacuated. The purpose is therefore to lay out the old requirements and then show a device that met none of them, which is what the final sentence about amplification inside the solid confirms.

whyWrong.A: The text never claims the vacuum tube stayed useful; it says nothing at all about what happened to tubes after 1947.
whyWrong.B: No products are mentioned. The passage stops at the laboratory result.
whyWrong.D: Doping is not discussed; the germanium is described only as a block that two contacts were pressed onto.

commonMistakes: Picking a purpose that is plausible about transistors in general rather than one supported by the sentences actually on the page.

whyCorrect: Track the sentences in order. The first describes inoculation as an established practice and says it worked; the second lists two costs — it killed a few and let those inoculated infect others; the third says Jenner's cowpox substitution kept the protection while removing both. That is exactly the practice, drawbacks, improvement sequence.

whyWrong.A: The severity comparison appears only in the last sentence as a supporting detail; it is not the shape of the whole text.
whyWrong.C: The spread into Europe is mentioned in a single clause and is never traced; the text moves to drawbacks instead.
whyWrong.D: Nothing is said about how contemporaries received Jenner's method.

tips: For structure questions, summarize each sentence in a few words first, then match the sequence to the choices.

whyCorrect: The final sentence does the work: the king drew his authority from the older town and the wealth that paid for it passed through the newer one. The two-town layout described earlier is the setup for that split, with the court and sacred grove in one place and the merchants, mosques and account-keepers in the other. The main idea is that the physical separation matched a separation between where power came from and where money came from.

whyWrong.A: The text never says the kings adopted Islam or gives any motive of securing merchant loyalty.
whyWrong.B: The scholars kept the accounts; the king taxed every load of salt, so control of the trade rests with him, not with them.
whyWrong.C: No dates or plans for the two settlements are given, so nothing supports their being laid out together.

commonMistakes: Choosing a detail from the middle of the passage instead of the claim the last sentence builds toward.

whyCorrect: The passage gives the observation first — diversity clusters in particular regions, wheat in the Caucasus and Near East, potatoes in the Andes — and then the proposal built on it: diversity is greatest where a crop was first domesticated. Read together, that is a method for locating an origin from a pattern of variety. Choice C states exactly that inference from where varieties are numerous to where domestication began.

whyWrong.A: The text says the opposite in its first sentence: varieties are not spread evenly.
whyWrong.B: The Andes are named only for potatoes; nothing claims they lead in every crop.
whyWrong.D: No dates are given for either domestication, so the passage cannot support a claim that they coincided.

tips: When a passage reports an observation and then a proposal, the main idea is usually the link between them, not either one alone.

whyCorrect: Duclos's claim is that twenty-metre spacing is too wide, so the supporting data has to connect distance to a loss of fruit set and reach out to the distances such spacing produces. The table falls steadily from 41 per cent under 6 m to 11 per cent beyond 18 m, and trees standing twenty metres apart leave flowers in exactly that worst band. Choice B cites both ends of that decline and ties them to the block's spacing.

whyWrong.A: The comparison is also inaccurate as arithmetic: 22 per cent against 41 per cent is a little over half, but it stops at the middle of the table and never reaches the distances a twenty-metre spacing creates.
whyWrong.C: The 34 per cent figure is a single mid-range value with nothing to compare it to, so it shows no decline at all.
whyWrong.D: The 11 per cent figure alone gives no baseline; without the 41 per cent near a pollinizer there is no evidence that distance is what lowered it.

commonMistakes: Quoting one true number from the table instead of the comparison that actually supports the claim.

whyCorrect: The manuscript has no colophon, so the argument for Saint-Amand has to rest on physical features of the book that are specific to one scriptorium. Ruling pattern, abbreviation system and letterforms are exactly such features, and the finding says all three match dated Saint-Amand books and none of them appears in books from the rival houses. That both confirms Saint-Amand and rules the others out.

whyWrong.B: Owning a copy of Boethius is not the same as producing this one; libraries acquired books from elsewhere constantly.
whyWrong.C: Calfskin was used by nearly every house of the period, so it distinguishes nothing.
whyWrong.D: Textual agreement with the northern French version points away from Saint-Amand if anything, and in any case a text could be copied anywhere from a northern French exemplar.

tips: Evidence that supports one candidate only counts if it also fails to fit the alternatives.

whyCorrect: Semmelweis claims a physical agent travels from the dissecting room on the students' hands. The finding that tests it is one that removes the agent and watches the deaths respond: after chlorine handwashing was required, mortality in that ward fell to the midwives' rate within months. That intervention-and-result pattern is what turns a correlation between staffing and deaths into evidence for the mechanism he proposed.

whyWrong.A: Fever elsewhere in Europe says nothing about what distinguishes the two Vienna wards from each other.
whyWrong.B: More anatomy instruction explains why students were in the dissecting room but supplies no evidence that anything was carried out of it.
whyWrong.D: Equal admissions rules out one alternative explanation for the raw death counts, but on its own it gives no support to the carrying claim.

commonMistakes: Choosing a fact that is consistent with the hypothesis over the one that would change if the hypothesis were false.

whyCorrect: The whole contrast in the passage is about the horizon of prediction: wind can be forecast a day or two out, tides can be tabulated years out. The blank has to name what that longer horizon gives a grid operator, and what an operator does with a known future output is plan the rest of the system around it. Choice D is the only option that is about advance knowledge rather than about the shape of the output.

whyWrong.A: Tidal output is not steady through the day — it rises and falls with the tide; the passage claims only that the variation is known in advance.
whyWrong.B: Predictable does not mean conveniently timed; a tidal station's peak may fall in the middle of the night.
whyWrong.C: Reserve plant is still needed, since the tidal station stops generating at slack water however well that is predicted.

tips: Predictable and constant are different properties; this passage argues only for the first.

whyCorrect: The passage sets up a trade-off between two sources of stride work: the tendon returns stored energy for free, while muscle must burn fuel. It then says the tendon's share rises as stride rate rises. Two runners at the same speed with different stride rates therefore split the work differently between the free source and the fuelled one, which is what choice B states.

whyWrong.A: Muscle recruitment counts are never discussed; the passage contrasts elastic return with fuel use, not how many muscles act.
whyWrong.C: Both runners hold one speed, so in a given time they cover the same distance by definition.
whyWrong.D: The passage attributes the difference to stride rate, not to any difference in the tendons themselves.

commonMistakes: Reading the conclusion as being about the tendons rather than about how the work of a stride is paid for.

whyCorrect: The subject is Foam landing beds and the main verb is allowed. Between them sits the nonrestrictive participial phrase introduced in the years just before the Mexico City Games, and the comma after beds has already opened it. A nonrestrictive modifier takes a comma at both ends, so a second comma is required after Games to close it.

whyWrong.A: With no closing comma the modifier is left open, since the opening comma after beds is never answered.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon joins two independent clauses; allowed a jumper to land on the shoulders in safety has no subject of its own.
whyWrong.D: A colon must follow a complete clause, and Foam landing beds, introduced in the years just before the Mexico City Games is not one.

tips: If you see a comma before a modifier, check that a matching comma closes it before the verb.

whyCorrect: Everything from since through absence is a subordinate clause explaining why the vessels are shaped as they are, and vessels are broad and shallow is the independent clause it attaches to. A subordinate clause placed in front of its main clause is closed with a comma, so the comma in choice D is the required mark.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon must have an independent clause on both sides, and since the organisms need air as much as the yeast before them needed its absence cannot stand alone.
whyWrong.B: A colon likewise requires a complete clause in front of it, and the since clause is not complete.
whyWrong.C: Adding and makes the vessels clause a second subordinate element inside since, leaving the sentence with no main clause after the conjunction.

commonMistakes: Treating any long stretch of words as an independent clause; a clause beginning with since never is one.

whyCorrect: Everything before the blank — what those works gathered was the one thing the fields could not otherwise get — is a complete sentence, and what follows names that one thing. A colon is the mark that introduces a naming element after a complete clause, so get: runoff is correct.

whyWrong.A: With no mark at all, runoff has no grammatical role: it cannot be the object of get, which already has the one thing as its object.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and runoff from an area of hillside many times the size of the plot it watered is only a noun phrase.
whyWrong.D: A comma is too weak to introduce the naming element here and leaves runoff reading as a loose fragment tacked onto the verb.

tips: Complete sentence, then a colon, then the thing the sentence has been pointing at — that pattern is tested constantly.

whyCorrect: Both halves stand alone: the whole ingot grows as a single crystal is one sentence, and a boule two metres long may contain no grain boundary at all is another. Two independent clauses with no conjunction between them require a semicolon.

whyWrong.A: Running crystal a boule together makes a boule look like part of the first clause, which produces nonsense.
whyWrong.B: A colon followed by and is not a construction English uses, and the second clause here explains rather than announces.
whyWrong.D: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.

commonMistakes: Assuming that because the second clause explains the first it must take a colon; a semicolon handles two full clauses in either relation.

whyCorrect: Find what the relative pronoun that stands for. It refers to the few in the array, not to array, so the verb in the relative clause is plural: the few that have never been cleaned. Choice C is the only plural form offered.

whyWrong.A: Is is singular and also the wrong tense for the participle been cleaned in this construction.
whyWrong.B: Has is singular; it would agree with array, but array is inside the prepositional phrase in the array and cannot be the subject.
whyWrong.D: Having is a participle, which leaves the relative clause with no finite verb at all.

tips: Strip the prepositional phrase — of the few in the array, only the few can be the subject.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with the participial phrase Checking those catchwords against the first words of each gathering, so whatever noun follows the comma has to be the one doing the checking. Only a person can check catchwords, and the cataloguer is the only person offered as a subject.

whyWrong.A: There did not check anything; the placeholder subject leaves the participle with nothing to attach to.
whyWrong.B: This makes the order of the book the checker, which the order cannot do.
whyWrong.C: This makes a misbound quire the checker, which is the same dangling-modifier error.

commonMistakes: Choosing the option whose meaning fits best and ignoring which noun lands right after the comma — that noun is what the opening phrase describes.

whyCorrect: The main clause is anchored in the past by By the time the cheesemaker cut into the first wheel. The rind's colour change finished before that moment, and the past perfect is what marks an action completed before another past action. That is also why the comparison with the earlier batches, which had never reached that colour, reads consistently.

whyWrong.A: Will turn puts the change in the future, which cannot follow a past-tense by the time clause.
whyWrong.B: Is turning is present progressive and clashes with cut.
whyWrong.C: Turns is simple present and describes a habitual or current fact, not something completed before a past moment.

tips: By the time plus a past-tense verb is the standard trigger for the past perfect in the other clause.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says planting works: marram traps the sand before it reaches the crest. The second sentence names the limit on that success — it lasts only while the roots do, and one drought can undo it. Moving from a method that works to the condition under which it fails is a contrast, so However is the right connector.

whyWrong.A: For instance would make the second sentence an example of successful planting, but it describes the planting failing.
whyWrong.C: Therefore claims the failure follows from the trapping, when nothing in the first sentence causes drought or root death.
whyWrong.D: Likewise signals a parallel point, and the second sentence reverses the first rather than matching it.

tips: Watch for holds only while — a limit stated on a claim just made almost always calls for a contrast.

whyCorrect: The same fact — water's density — is presented twice with opposite value. In the first sentence density is the advantage that lets small blades harvest a slow current; in the second it is the burden that forces heavier construction. A connector marking that reversal is needed, and However is the only one offered.

whyWrong.B: For example would make the loading on the blades an instance of drawing power efficiently, which it is not.
whyWrong.C: Similarly signals agreement between the two sentences, but the second states a cost against the first's benefit.
whyWrong.D: As a result would make the heavy loading a consequence of the smaller blades, when the passage attributes it directly to density.

commonMistakes: Seeing the same cause named in both sentences and reaching for a cause-and-effect transition; here the shared cause has opposite consequences.

whyCorrect: The first sentence describes the parts of a wall that rain reaches: they are washed clean. The second describes the parts rain does not reach — under a cornice, behind a column — and they do the opposite, gathering a damaging black crust. Two parts of the same facade behaving in opposite ways calls for By contrast.

whyWrong.B: Consequently would make the black crust a result of the washing, but the crust forms precisely where washing does not happen.
whyWrong.C: In addition presents the second fact as a further similar point rather than as the opposite case.
whyWrong.D: For example would make sheltered stonework an instance of being washed clean, which reverses the meaning.

tips: When a passage splits one object into exposed and sheltered halves, expect a contrast connector between them.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain why 32,768 hertz specifically was chosen, so the sentence has to link that number to something that makes it useful. The notes supply the link: 32,768 is two raised to the fifteenth power, and fifteen successive halvings of it give exactly one pulse per second. Choice C is the only option that puts the power of two together with the fifteen halving stages, which is what turns the number from arbitrary into convenient.

whyWrong.A: Comparing the crystal with a mechanical balance says the frequency is high but gives no reason for that particular value.
whyWrong.B: This states the frequency and the halving chain but omits the power-of-two fact, so it never explains why 32,768 rather than any other number.
whyWrong.D: This describes how a quartz crystal works at all and does not mention the frequency.

tips: For a why question, check that the sentence contains the fact that does the explaining, not just the fact being explained.

whyCorrect: The goal names a cause-and-consequence link: the fix for the first outbreak is what exposed the industry to the second. Choice A supplies both halves — growers swapped one clonal variety for another, so Cavendish plantations are as genetically uniform as Gros Michel ones were, and a new strain is now moving through them. The uniformity note is what makes the replacement a repeat of the original vulnerability rather than a solution.

whyWrong.B: This covers only the first outbreak and never reaches the second or the reason the two are connected.
whyWrong.C: The propagation fact alone is the mechanism with no outbreak attached to it, so no explanation is made.
whyWrong.D: This states the second outbreak but not why the response to the first left the industry open to it.

commonMistakes: Picking a true sentence that repeats one note; a synthesis question needs the notes that together answer the stated goal.

whyCorrect: What the 1951 design changed can only be shown by a comparison, since a change is relative to what came before. Choice B states the new method — habits recorded first, deaths matched to them as they occurred — and sets it against the earlier practice of questioning patients who were already ill. That contrast is precisely the design change the goal asks for.

whyWrong.A: Matching deaths to habits describes part of the new method but never mentions what it replaced.
whyWrong.C: The size of the mailing and the response rate are facts about scale, not about design.
whyWrong.D: This gives only the older approach, so the reader cannot see what was new.

tips: When a goal asks what a study changed, the answer nearly always has to name both the old approach and the new one.

whyCorrect: The colon after the blank means the rest of the sentence defines it, and what follows is a comparison of two clock times: the same bright light shifts the clock measurably before bed and hardly at all at noon. A quantity whose size changes with the hour is one that depends on timing, which is what choice C says.

whyWrong.A: Nothing restricts the effect to a laboratory; the example given is ordinary screen light before bed.
whyWrong.B: The example after the colon states directly that the effect differs between evening and noon, so it is not the same all day.
whyWrong.D: Negligible contradicts shifts the following night's timing measurably.

tips: After a colon, read the example first and pick the phrase it is illustrating.

whyCorrect: The two failure modes given after the colon are both about when the process is stopped: halted too early gives too little enzyme, halted too late leaves nothing for the brewer. Both errors are errors of moment, not of size or heat, so the word in the blank has to be timing.

whyWrong.A: Scale would concern how much barley is malted, which neither failure mode mentions.
whyWrong.C: Heat appears in the passage as the means of stopping the sprout, but the failures described are about stopping too soon or too late, not too hot or too cold.
whyWrong.D: Cleanliness is never raised in the passage at all.

commonMistakes: Choosing temperature because heat is mentioned nearby; the blank has to be defined by the two failures listed after the colon.

whyCorrect: Steel springs change stiffness with temperature, which is why a watch adjusted in a warm room ran fast in winter. Guillaume's alloy holds its stiffness across the temperature range, so the fault disappears: the rate no longer responds to the weather. Unaffected is the word for that loss of influence.

whyWrong.A: Obscured would mean the rate became hard to observe, but the problem was that it changed, not that it was hidden.
whyWrong.B: Improved by the weather makes no sense as a description of an influence being removed.
whyWrong.D: Governed says the weather still controls the rate, which is exactly the old steel-spring behaviour the alloy eliminates.

tips: When a passage names a problem and then a fix, the blank usually states the absence of the problem.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the underlined word describes exactly what a sport is: one branch on an otherwise uniform tree bearing fruit that ripens earlier or colours more deeply than the rest. The next sentence adds that if the shoot keeps that character when grafted, it becomes a new variety. So sport here means a shoot that differs from the tree it grew on.

whyWrong.A: This is the everyday sense of the word and has nothing to do with grafting or fruit.
whyWrong.C: A good sport describes a person, but the passage's sport is grafted onto rootstock.
whyWrong.D: A display for attention does not fit a branch that nurseries propagate.

commonMistakes: Reaching for the familiar meaning of a common word; the surrounding sentences define the technical sense being tested.

whyCorrect: The passage separates the two jobs cleanly: the root fixes the size of the tree but leaves the fruit unchanged, and the grafted variety fixes the fruit. Because neither determines the other, a grower can pair any variety with any rootstock, which is what independent of states.

whyWrong.B: Identical to would mean the two decisions are one decision, but the passage says the same variety behaves differently on different stocks.
whyWrong.C: Dictated by makes the fruit determine the root, contradicting the statement that the root leaves the fruit unchanged.
whyWrong.D: A consequence of is the same error in different words: it makes one choice follow from the other when the passage keeps them apart.

tips: When a text says one factor leaves another unchanged, the relationship word you want is one of independence.

whyCorrect: The text opens with a general claim — a workshop can work only to the accuracy of its standards — and closes with a change: machinists who once trusted a rule and a practised eye could now set a tool against a physical length. The underlined sentence supplies what made that change possible, describing the stackable steel blocks that give any dimension to within a fraction of a micrometre. Its function is to introduce those standards so the closing change has a cause.

whyWrong.B: The adhesion of two blocks is a separate sentence, and the underlined sentence offers no explanation of why it happens.
whyWrong.C: The underlined sentence raises no question; the comparison with a practised eye comes later and is stated, not questioned.
whyWrong.D: No market, sales or commercial context appears anywhere in the text.

tips: For function questions, read what comes after the underlined sentence — the function is usually its relation to that.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences give altitude a benefit and a cost: more red cells, but slower training because less oxygen reaches the muscle. The third sentence gives the resolution — sleep high, train low — which takes the benefit while dodging the cost. The text exists to lay out that conflict and its workaround.

whyWrong.B: The text credits altitude with raising red cell counts, so it does not deny an advantage.
whyWrong.C: The mechanism of red cell production is never described; the passage only reports that the count rises.
whyWrong.D: No elevation is specified and nothing is recommended to any individual athlete.

commonMistakes: Naming one half of the passage as the purpose; here the purpose is the pairing of the conflict with the arrangement that resolves it.

whyCorrect: The passage draws a distinction between two fabrics in the same rock: the cleavage, produced when mountain building squeezed the clay minerals into alignment, and the original sedimentary bedding. It says explicitly that the two have nothing to do with each other and often cross, and that the splitter follows the cleavage. That is the main idea choice C states.

whyWrong.A: No preference of any quarry is mentioned; the passage says the two directions often run across each other and treats that as normal.
whyWrong.B: This reverses the passage: the alignment comes from later squeezing during mountain building, not from settling mud.
whyWrong.D: The few millimetres figure is an incidental detail about how thin slate splits, not a standard being described.

tips: When a text keeps two similar-sounding features apart, the main idea is usually the distinction itself.

whyCorrect: The passage explains the physical construction — sheets folded, gathered and sewn through the fold, so the first and last pages of a gathering are one sheet — and then draws the consequence: a scribe had to judge the length of the text in advance, because a long passage could not gain an extra leaf without disturbing the gathering. The main idea is that link from construction to planning.

whyWrong.B: The first sentence denies this: a medieval book was not written page by page in reading order.
whyWrong.C: Strength is never compared; the passage discusses gathering size only in terms of how sheets were folded.
whyWrong.D: The passage assigns the judgement of length to the scribe copying the text, not to the binder.

commonMistakes: Picking the sentence that describes the physical method and stopping there, instead of the consequence the passage builds to.

whyCorrect: Fanning's claim is that oxygen saving tracks energy return, not material family. Supporting it needs two foams at opposite ends of the return column shown to sit at opposite ends of the oxygen column: the polyether block amide returns 87 per cent and costs the least at 199, while conventional EVA returns 66 per cent and costs the most at 213. Choice B pairs both variables for both extremes, which is what shows the tracking.

whyWrong.A: This gives the worst oxygen cost with no energy-return figure beside it, so no relationship between the two columns is demonstrated.
whyWrong.C: Comparing the two EVAs on return alone leaves out oxygen cost entirely, and staying inside one material family cannot test a claim about crossing families.
whyWrong.D: This compares two foams on return only, and their oxygen costs of 201 and 199 are nearly identical, which illustrates nothing about the trend.

tips: A claim that one measure tracks another needs both measures quoted, usually at the two extremes.

whyCorrect: Arrieta has to beat a specific rival explanation: that the missing parent was a European yeast now extinct. Genetic distance settles it — if the lager genome's non-ale half is only a few centuries diverged from the Patagonian species and far more diverged from every European yeast sequenced, then the Patagonian species is the close relative and the European candidates are not. Choice A supplies exactly that two-sided comparison.

whyWrong.B: Cold tolerance makes the Patagonian species a plausible candidate but does not distinguish it from any other cold-tolerant yeast, including a European one.
whyWrong.C: A date for the first record of lager brewing says nothing about which organism supplied half the genome.
whyWrong.D: How easily hybrids form in the laboratory is about the mechanism, not about which species was the parent.

commonMistakes: Accepting evidence that fits the favoured hypothesis without checking whether it also fits the alternative.

whyCorrect: Kruse's claim sets two explanations against each other, so the data has to show a pattern that hours on duty cannot produce. On the night shift the rate rises to 6.8 at five to six hours — around 04:00 to 05:00 — and then falls to 5.2 with more hours worked, while the day shift climbs steadily across the same span. A rate that falls as duty lengthens cannot be driven by duty length, and the peak lands at the hour the internal clock is calling hardest for sleep.

whyWrong.A: The night shift's higher rate in its first two hours shows a difference between the shifts, but the whole night column is higher, so this alone is consistent with night workers simply being worse at every duration.
whyWrong.B: The day shift's steady climb with hours on duty is evidence for the explanation Kruse is arguing against.
whyWrong.C: Noting that every figure is under seven ignores the pattern entirely and supports neither explanation.

tips: When a claim says X rather than Y, look for the data point where Y predicts one thing and the table shows another.

whyCorrect: The passage says granite parts more readily along the grain than across it, and that the row of holes is what steers the break. Splitting across the grain therefore means the wedges are working against the rock's preferred direction, and the line of weakness the holes create has to be made stronger to win — which means putting the holes closer together. Choice B is the only option that adjusts the method to the added difficulty.

whyWrong.A: If drilling made no difference to direction, quarrymen could not split blocks to a chosen line at all, which contradicts the whole procedure described.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the text links the smoothness of the face to grain direction; the property described is ease of parting.
whyWrong.D: This reverses the passage, which says granite parts more readily along the grain, so a cross-grain line takes more effort, not less.

commonMistakes: Treating the harder direction as somehow better; the text only ranks the directions by how readily the rock parts.

whyCorrect: The passage says these seeds are killed by the drying itself, before freezing is ever reached, and that no care at the freezing stage can undo the damage. That rules out any adjustment to the standard routine, because the fatal step is the routine's first step. The only conclusion left is that such species must be kept some other way entirely, which is choice C.

whyWrong.A: The problem is not the temperature; the embryo is already dead from drying before the packet is frozen.
whyWrong.B: Collecting more often does not preserve anything, and nothing in the passage compares collection frequency.
whyWrong.D: Drying more slowly is still drying, and the passage says the damage happens as the last of the water leaves, however it leaves.

tips: When a text says a step is fatal and a later step cannot rescue it, the inference is to abandon the method, not to tune it.

whyCorrect: The subject is Michelangelo and the main verb is left. Between them sits the nonrestrictive relative clause who spent months in the quarries choosing stone before he would begin a figure, and the comma after Michelangelo has opened it. Such a clause takes a comma at both ends, so a comma is required after figure to close it.

whyWrong.A: Without the closing comma the relative clause is never shut, and the opening comma after Michelangelo is left unmatched.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon needs an independent clause on each side, and left blocks rejected on the mountain has no subject.
whyWrong.D: A colon must be preceded by a complete clause, and Michelangelo, who spent months in the quarries choosing stone before he would begin a figure is not one.

commonMistakes: Hearing a natural pause and choosing a heavier mark; what the sentence needs is simply the second half of a comma pair.

whyCorrect: A dash has already opened before a pointing hand, and the list that follows is an interruption between the subject Every kind of mark and its verb suggests. Punctuation used in pairs must match, so the interruption has to close with a second dash. Using a dash also keeps the internal commas of the list from being mistaken for the boundary.

whyWrong.B: A comma cannot close a dash; the pair would be mismatched, and it would also blend into the commas already separating the listed items.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon cannot close a parenthetical interruption, and what follows it is not an independent clause.
whyWrong.D: A colon would announce something new rather than close the list, leaving the opening dash unanswered.

tips: Dash-comma and comma-dash are never valid pairs; whichever mark opens the interruption has to close it.

whyCorrect: Everything from Because through scale is a subordinate clause giving the reason, and casters cast them as beetles, sandals, drums and knotted cords is the main clause. An introductory subordinate clause is separated from the main clause by a comma.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon requires an independent clause before it, and a clause beginning with Because is not independent.
whyWrong.B: A colon likewise needs a complete clause in front of it, which the Because clause is not.
whyWrong.C: Adding and turns the main clause into a second element governed by Because, which leaves the sentence with no independent clause at all.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that Because at the front of a sentence makes everything up to the comma subordinate, no matter how long it runs.

whyCorrect: The word which here refers back to the whole preceding statement — that a ship still healthy after forty days really was safe — and introduces a nonrestrictive relative clause commenting on it. A nonrestrictive which clause attaches to the sentence with a comma.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause; which was a piece of luck begins with a relative pronoun and cannot stand alone.
whyWrong.B: A colon introduces a naming or explaining element, not a relative clause, and the same dependency problem applies.
whyWrong.C: Ending the sentence at safe leaves Which was a piece of luck nobody at the time was in a position to know about as a fragment.

tips: A clause opening with which is dependent; it joins with a comma, never a semicolon or a period.

whyCorrect: What is being compared is the wear on one drive's bearings with the wear on the other's. Wear is singular, so the pronoun standing in for it in the second half of the comparison is the singular that: roughly double that found on the drive that stayed cool.

whyWrong.B: Those is plural and would have to stand for a plural noun; the sentence compares wear, not bearings.
whyWrong.C: Them cannot be modified by a participial phrase in this position and does not work in a comparison of quantities.
whyWrong.D: Which would open a relative clause describing the wear on the hotter drive, which destroys the comparison the sentence is making.

tips: In comparisons, use that for a singular noun and those for a plural one — check which noun is actually being compared.

whyCorrect: The subject is Each, not engines; of the three engines in the workshop is a prepositional phrase and cannot supply the subject. Each is always singular, so the verb is has.

whyWrong.B: Having is a participle and leaves the sentence with no main verb.
whyWrong.C: Were having is plural and past progressive, wrong in both number and tense for a standing description.
whyWrong.D: Have is the plural form, which agrees with engines rather than with the actual subject Each.

commonMistakes: Letting the plural noun nearest the verb set the agreement; cross out the of phrase and the subject Each is obvious.

whyCorrect: The subject is The number, a singular noun; of such hours a variety requires is a modifier sitting between it and the verb. A singular subject in the present takes ranges.

whyWrong.A: Range is the plural present form and agrees with hours, which is inside the modifier rather than the subject.
whyWrong.C: Have ranged is plural and puts the fact in the present perfect, when the sentence states a standing property of varieties.
whyWrong.D: Are ranging is plural and progressive, describing something in progress rather than a fixed range of requirements.

tips: Number of X is singular when it names a quantity: the number ranges, a number of varieties range.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences say the doubling was a target rather than a law of physics, and that the whole supply chain planned to one published schedule. The sentence after the blank says the pace was a prediction the industry arranged to fulfil — the same claim compressed into one line. A restatement takes In other words.

whyWrong.A: For instance would require a specific case, but the sentence generalizes rather than giving an example.
whyWrong.B: Meanwhile marks something happening at the same time elsewhere; the sentence adds no new event.
whyWrong.D: Nevertheless signals a concession, and the sentence agrees with what precedes it instead of pushing against it.

tips: If a sentence contains no new fact, it is a restatement — reach for In other words or That is.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the rule: daily light resets the clock, and without it the clock free-runs on a cycle slightly longer than twenty-four hours. The second sentence gives what happens to people who receive no light at all — their sleep drifts in and out of phase with the calendar. That is the predicted result of the rule, so a consequence marker is needed.

whyWrong.A: Nevertheless would set the drifting sleep against the first sentence, but the drifting is exactly what the first sentence predicts.
whyWrong.B: Similarly compares two parallel cases, and only one case is described here.
whyWrong.C: In contrast requires an opposition, and the second sentence confirms rather than opposes the first.

commonMistakes: Reading the odd fortnight-on, fortnight-off pattern as surprising and choosing a contrast; it is the direct outcome of a clock running long.

whyCorrect: The second sentence lists the costs of countersinking: more expensive to build, harder to repair. The third says high-speed aircraft are countersunk anyway. Doing something despite its stated drawbacks is a concession, which is what Nonetheless marks; the because clause then supplies the justification.

whyWrong.A: Consequently would make countersinking the result of its own added cost and difficulty, which is backwards.
whyWrong.B: Likewise signals a parallel point, but the third sentence overrides the second rather than matching it.
whyWrong.C: In short introduces a summary, and the third sentence brings in a new fact — universal practice — rather than condensing what came before.

tips: Drawbacks stated, then the practice continued anyway, means a concession transition.

whyCorrect: The goal asks why the rules limit throws instead of speed. The answer needs the note that damage accumulates across many throws, joined to the note that a single pitch already runs close to the ligament's failure strength — together those explain why counting throws is the lever available. Choice A links both to the pitch counts and rest days the leagues adopted.

whyWrong.B: Naming the ligament's function is background and offers no reason for the choice of rule.
whyWrong.C: The torque figure alone would argue for limiting velocity, not throw counts, since it concerns a single maximum-effort pitch.
whyWrong.D: This restates the rules without explaining why they take that form.

tips: When a goal asks why a policy targets X rather than Y, the sentence has to contain the reason, not just the policy.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain how salting selects the organisms that ferment. Choice B gives the whole selection: the brine drawn from the leaves excludes most soil bacteria, and the salt-tolerant lactic acid bacteria multiply in it and acidify the vessel. Both halves are needed, since selection means one group blocked and another favoured.

whyWrong.A: The origin of the bacteria in soil is background; it does not describe what salting does to them.
whyWrong.C: The order of operations tells the reader when salting happens but nothing about its effect on the microbial population.
whyWrong.D: Acidification is what happens after the selection has occurred, so it describes a consequence rather than the selecting step.

commonMistakes: Choosing the note about acid because it sounds like the important chemistry; the question asks about the stage that decides who is present to make it.

whyCorrect: The difficulty named in the goal is distance, so the sentence must connect the reforms to the problem of governing a thousand miles of river. Choice D pairs the administrative change — appointed governors in place of hereditary lords — with the fleet that cut transit from weeks to days, and states the result as one administration over that distance. It is the only choice that names both a reform and the distance problem it answers.

whyWrong.A: This states the difficulty alone and mentions no reform.
whyWrong.B: The ministries are a reform, but the sentence never connects them to the size of the territory.
whyWrong.C: Standard weights serve trade in the markets and do not address distance or the control of provinces.

tips: A how-did-this-address-that question needs both halves in one sentence: the problem and the mechanism.

whyCorrect: The passage defines the term before using it: each arriving lot is a handful from one farmer's field in one season, numbered and stored apart from every other lot. The reason given for keeping them separate is that two collections of one named variety may differ genetically. So an accession is an individually kept sample, which is choice C.

whyWrong.A: An increase in quantity would describe the growth of the bank, but the sentence counts half a million discrete items, not an amount added.
whyWrong.B: Coming to a throne is the historical sense of the word and has no bearing on stored seed.
whyWrong.D: Joining a treaty is the diplomatic sense; nothing in the passage involves states or agreements.

commonMistakes: Choosing a dictionary sense that exists rather than the one the surrounding sentences have just defined.

whyCorrect: The colon after the blank explains it: a wide shallow system takes up a large share of a brief soaking before the water drains or evaporates. That is a match between the root design and the rainfall pattern just described, so the blank has to express fit. Well suited to is the only choice that does.

whyWrong.A: Indifferent to would mean the rainfall pattern makes no difference to the roots, but the passage explains how the roots exploit it.
whyWrong.B: Opposed to reverses the relationship, making the roots work against the pattern they are adapted to.
whyWrong.C: Prior to is a claim about time, and the sentence is comparing form with conditions, not sequence.

tips: Read past the colon first: the explanation tells you what the blank has to mean.

whyCorrect: The clause after the blank says what an airborne cause would have produced: deaths thinning out evenly in every direction from a source of stench. What Snow actually found was a tight cluster around one pump, which is the opposite distribution. The blank therefore has to say the pattern sits badly with the airborne account, and difficult to reconcile with is the only phrase that does.

whyWrong.A: Readily explained by makes the cluster a natural result of foul air, but the sentence itself says airborne spread would have thinned out evenly instead.
whyWrong.C: Consistent with says the evidence fits the airborne account, which the rest of the sentence directly denies.
whyWrong.D: Indistinguishable from would mean the pattern could not tell the two explanations apart, when the whole point is that it does.

tips: When a which clause spells out what a hypothesis predicts and the data differ, the blank must express conflict.

whyCorrect: The problem stated first is that a reader trained on one region's script struggled with another's. The features of the new hand — separated letters, uniform height, spaces between words — all make text easier to decipher, and the clause after the colon says a book in this hand could be read anywhere. The blank names the aim that all of this serves, which is legibility.

whyWrong.A: Novelty would make newness the goal, but the passage measures the hand by whether it can be read.
whyWrong.B: Secrecy is the reverse of the stated aim of being readable everywhere.
whyWrong.D: Economy would concern saving parchment or time, and the described features — wide spacing, uniform letters — do not save material.

commonMistakes: Choosing a plausible motive for a reform instead of the one the sentence after the colon spells out.

whyCorrect: The passage sets the problem up before it names it: every block must lay ink exactly where the previous one left the paper clear, and the corner mark and notch exist so the sheet lands identically at each pass. What holds through a dozen impressions is therefore the exact fit of one colour to the ones already printed, which is choice A.

whyWrong.B: The musical sense of register has nothing to do with blocks and paper.
whyWrong.C: A heating grate is another sense of the word and is unrelated to printing.
whyWrong.D: A formal list is the most common everyday sense, but no record is being kept here; the marks control alignment.

tips: Technical vocabulary questions are answered by the sentence explaining the problem, not by the most familiar meaning.

whyCorrect: The final sentence states a consequence: lose the palms and the plots beneath fail within a few seasons. The underlined sentence is what makes that consequence intelligible, since it says the palms are the condition of the other crops, cutting the sun and slowing the wind that would strip moisture from the leaves below. Its function is to supply the mechanism the last sentence depends on.

whyWrong.A: Value is mentioned only to be set aside — the palms are not the most valuable crop — so comparison of prices is not the point.
whyWrong.B: No species of fruit tree is named anywhere in the text.
whyWrong.C: Nothing concedes difficulty of maintenance; the sentence explains a benefit rather than admitting a cost.

tips: When the underlined sentence sits just before a consequence, its function is almost always to explain why that consequence follows.

whyCorrect: The text runs in sequence: two aircraft broke up, investigators rebuilt a fuselage and cycled it in a water tank until it split, the crack was traced to a window corner where repeated pressurisation concentrated stress, and later aircraft used rounded openings. That is an investigation and its outcome, which is what choice D states.

whyWrong.A: No judgement about readiness is offered; the text reports what was found, not that anyone was at fault.
whyWrong.B: Cabin pressurisation is mentioned only as the source of the repeated stress, and no principle of it is explained.
whyWrong.C: Piston aircraft are never mentioned.

commonMistakes: Turning a factual account of an investigation into an argument; the text draws no blame and offers no thesis.

whyCorrect: The passage says the same boiled resins produce both the bitterness and the hostility to lactic bacteria, so a brewer selecting for one gets the other automatically. The final sentence makes the point explicit: brewers selecting for bitterness were selecting for keeping quality without knowing it. Choice B captures both the link and the ignorance of it.

whyWrong.A: Deliberately contradicts the passage, which stresses that hops were used long before anyone knew what they did.
whyWrong.C: Hops as the only preservative available is a claim the text never makes; other methods are not discussed.
whyWrong.D: The passage limits lactic bacteria to souring beer in cask and says nothing about other fermented drinks.

tips: When a text ends with without knowing it, the main idea usually turns on the gap between practice and understanding.

whyCorrect: Each detail in the passage feeds the same conclusion: waves move water in the chamber, the water pushes air through a duct, the turbine there turns the same way in either direction so no valve is needed, and the only moving part sits above the water out of the sea's reach. The main idea is that this chain of conversions is what keeps the machinery clear of seawater.

whyWrong.A: The passage says the opposite — the turbine is built to turn the same way whichever way the air moves, so it is never reversed.
whyWrong.C: Wave height and power output are never discussed, let alone as a proportional relation.
whyWrong.D: The text notes that no valve is needed but makes no claim about valves being the likeliest component to fail.

commonMistakes: Picking a technically plausible statement about wave power that the passage itself never asserts.

whyCorrect: Sethi is not arguing that the planar process helped; he is arguing about which part of it mattered, the surviving oxide rather than the patterning it enabled. Only a comparison that isolates the oxide can settle that. Choice C does it directly: identical devices with the oxide stripped drift like the old ones, while those keeping it hold their characteristics, so the oxide layer itself is what stabilises the device.

whyWrong.A: How easily oxide can be grown is a fact about manufacture and says nothing about which benefit dominated.
whyWrong.B: Improved yields follow from the process as a whole and do not separate the oxide from the patterning.
whyWrong.D: Connecting several transistors over the oxide is the patterning benefit, so this supports the position Sethi is arguing against.

tips: For a claim that X mattered more than Y, look for the finding that holds Y constant and varies X.

whyCorrect: Cierva's claim is about where the fix belongs — at the blade root rather than in the pilot's hands. The finding that tests it changes only the blade root and watches the rolling stop: hinged blades free to rise and fall took off cleanly while otherwise identical rigid blades still rolled. That comparison isolates the root mounting as the thing that relieves the imbalance.

whyWrong.A: Rotor speed compared with a helicopter's says nothing about an imbalance between advancing and retreating blades.
whyWrong.B: That the roll came on too fast to catch argues the pilot cannot fix it, but it offers no evidence that a change at the root can.
whyWrong.C: The lift-squared relation explains why the imbalance exists; it does not show where the remedy has to go.

commonMistakes: Choosing the option that rules out the rival half of the claim and stopping there — the argument also has to be shown to work.

whyCorrect: Okonjo's claim pits metabolic water from oxidising food against water the seeds absorbed from the air, so the decisive test removes the absorbed moisture and sees whether the animal still copes. Choice D does exactly that: rats fed seed dried to constant weight in air below five per cent humidity held their body mass just as well as rats given damp-burrow seed. With no absorbed water available and no deficit appearing, the water must be coming from the food's oxidation.

whyWrong.A: Seeds taking up water in a burrow supports the alternative explanation Okonjo is arguing against.
whyWrong.B: Concentrated urine shows the animal conserves water well but says nothing about where the water originates.
whyWrong.C: Foraging at night explains reduced losses in cool air, not the source of the water taken in.

tips: To support one of two competing sources, look for the experiment that takes the other source away.

whyCorrect: The passage builds a chain: a brass bearing wears oval, an oval hole lets the pivot wander off centre, and a wandering centre spoils the regularity the rate depends on. Ruby is far harder and holds a polish, so it resists that wear. What the maker buys is therefore a rate that stays accurate for far longer than it would on brass.

whyWrong.B: Ruby bearings are a refinement, and the passage gives no cost figures; nothing suggests they are cheaper.
whyWrong.C: Winding interval depends on the mainspring and the going train, not on the wear of a pivot bearing.
whyWrong.D: Magnetism is never mentioned, and hardness has nothing to do with magnetic shielding.

commonMistakes: Stopping at hardness as the benefit; the passage makes hardness a means and timekeeping accuracy the end.

whyCorrect: The middle sentence supplies the rule: strength comes from the number of points at which fibres cross and cling. Long fibres cross many times even when few of them are present, so a thin sheet of long-fibred paper still has plenty of those crossings. The conclusion the passage has set up is therefore about strength surviving thinness.

whyWrong.B: Ink absorption is never discussed, and a thinner sheet would if anything hold less.
whyWrong.C: No costs appear in the passage; the comparison is about fibre length and strength.
whyWrong.D: Yellowing concerns the chemistry of the pulp over time, which the passage does not raise.

tips: The sentence stating a general principle is usually the one the blank has to be derived from.

whyCorrect: Both halves are complete sentences: the orchards planted for the press are quite unlike the orchards planted for the table, and the trees in them would disappoint anyone who picked one. With no coordinating conjunction between them, a semicolon is the mark that joins them.

whyWrong.A: Running table the trees together produces a run-on and briefly reads as the table the, which garbles the sense.
whyWrong.B: A colon followed by and is not a valid construction, and the second clause continues the thought rather than announcing something.
whyWrong.D: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.

tips: Test each side of the blank on its own — if both stand alone and there is no conjunction, the answer is the semicolon.

whyCorrect: A pilot flies from one column to the next is a complete clause, and the aircraft climbs in each of them and gives most of that height back on the glide to the next is another. Two independent clauses with no coordinating conjunction take a semicolon.

whyWrong.A: With nothing between them the two clauses run together, leaving the aircraft momentarily reading as part of the first clause.
whyWrong.B: A colon plus and is not a construction English uses, and the second clause elaborates rather than introduces.
whyWrong.D: A comma alone between two independent clauses is a comma splice.

commonMistakes: Assuming a semicolon is only for unrelated sentences; closely connected clauses take one too when no conjunction is present.

whyCorrect: Nothing about the flight itself alters that rate of adjustment is one independent clause and for a few days after landing the traveller is living on two schedules at once is another. When two independent clauses are joined by the coordinating conjunction and, a comma goes before the conjunction.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon and a coordinating conjunction do the same joining work; using both together is redundant and incorrect here.
whyWrong.C: A colon introduces a naming or explaining element and cannot be followed by and in this way.
whyWrong.D: Omitting the comma before and joining two full clauses leaves the boundary unmarked, and the reader briefly attaches for a few days after landing to the first clause.

tips: Comma before and only when a full clause with its own subject and verb follows.

whyCorrect: The lever escapement does two things at once is a complete clause, and what follows is the pair it has just promised: a push delivered to the balance and a count of the swings. A colon after a complete clause is the mark that introduces such a list.

whyWrong.B: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and a small push delivered to the balance at every swing is a noun phrase.
whyWrong.C: Adding and makes the push a second item coordinated with the whole preceding clause, which breaks the promise of two things and leaves the list unbalanced.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation the noun phrase collides with the clause and once a small push reads as a time expression.

tips: A clause that announces a number of things — two things, three reasons — is nearly always followed by a colon.

whyCorrect: The sheaths belong to all six discs, so the possessor is plural. A plural noun already ending in s takes just an apostrophe after the s, giving discs' sheaths.

whyWrong.A: Disc's is singular possessive and would mean the sheaths of one disc, contradicting all six.
whyWrong.C: Discs's adds a second s to a plural that already ends in one, which is not standard.
whyWrong.D: Discs is a plain plural with no possessive marking, so the sentence would read as inspecting all six discs sheaths, with no relation between the two nouns.

tips: Decide how many owners there are first; the apostrophe goes after whatever plural or singular form names them.

whyCorrect: The subject is the seat's main charge, a singular noun. Along with the drogue gun and the two barostatic timers is a parenthetical phrase, and along with does not create a compound subject the way and would, so the number does not change. The verb stays singular: is replaced.

whyWrong.A: Are is plural and agrees with the items inside the along with phrase rather than with the subject.
whyWrong.B: Have been is plural and shifts to the present perfect, which does not fit a standing rule about what happens after every firing.
whyWrong.D: Were is plural and past, describing particular past events rather than the invariable practice the sentence states.

commonMistakes: Treating along with, as well as and together with like and; they add information without adding to the subject.

whyCorrect: The brief is given as a list of three tasks, and the first two are infinitives: to license the additive, to persuade the salt companies. Items in a series have to take the same grammatical form, so the third must be to measure the result.

whyWrong.A: Having measured is a perfect participle and breaks the series, besides putting the measuring before the other tasks.
whyWrong.B: Measuring is a gerund and does not match the two infinitives it is listed beside.
whyWrong.D: It measured introduces a new subject and a finite verb, turning the third item into a clause tacked onto a list of phrases.

tips: Find the first item in the list and copy its form exactly — parallelism questions are settled by matching, not by ear.

whyCorrect: The first sentence establishes that flat-foldability can be checked by counting mountain and valley folds at each vertex, before any paper is folded. The second draws what follows from that: a designer can verify a crease pattern on a computer and never touch paper. The second is the practical consequence of the first, so a cause-and-effect marker is needed.

whyWrong.A: Similarly would present the design workflow as a parallel case, but it is a result of the rule rather than an analogue of it.
whyWrong.C: By contrast requires opposition, and the two sentences agree completely.
whyWrong.D: Even so concedes something in spite of the first sentence, when the second in fact depends on it.

tips: A rule stated, then what the rule lets you do, is cause and effect.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank makes a general claim: banks guard against lost viability by testing rather than trusting storage. What follows is one bank's specific routine — sampling every accession on a cycle, sowing trays, counting germination, regrowing anything under about eighty-five per cent. A general policy followed by one institution's implementation of it calls for For example.

whyWrong.A: In contrast would set the national collection against the practice of testing, but its routine is that practice.
whyWrong.B: Consequently would make the sampling routine a result of the general policy rather than an illustration of it; the passage is naming an instance, not tracing an effect.
whyWrong.D: Nevertheless signals a concession, and nothing in the second sentence works against the first.

commonMistakes: Choosing Consequently whenever a second sentence follows naturally; ask whether it is caused by the first or is simply a case of it.

whyCorrect: The two sentences set two kinds of training against each other on the same measures. Continuous moderate running builds the heart and capillaries but leaves the fastest fibres unused; short fast repetitions recruit those fibres every time but cover far less ground. Opposite strengths and opposite costs call for By contrast.

whyWrong.A: Consequently would make interval training a result of continuous running, which it is not.
whyWrong.B: In addition would present the second method as a further point in the same direction, ignoring that it fixes the first method's gap and gives up its advantage.
whyWrong.C: For example would make the repetition session an instance of continuous moderate running, which it is the opposite of.

tips: When each sentence names a benefit the other lacks, the transition is a contrast.

whyCorrect: The goal asks how one operation explains both the surface and the strength, so the sentence must trace a single act to two results. Choice D does: the knapper's strike leaves one flat glassy face, that face goes outward to make the surface, and the rough back of the same stone is bedded in the mortar that binds the wall. Both outcomes are tied to the one blow.

whyWrong.A: This describes the raw material and mentions neither the operation nor its two effects.
whyWrong.B: Setting the knapped faces outward accounts for the surface only and leaves the strength unexplained.
whyWrong.C: This states the appearance of the finished wall and says nothing about how it holds together.

tips: When a goal names two outcomes, count them in the answer — a choice covering only one cannot be right.

whyCorrect: The goal is specifically about water spent on cooling. The relevant notes are the ones about temperature: instead of sweating to stay at a constant temperature, the camel lets its temperature climb several degrees by day and dumps that heat at night, when losing it costs no water. Choice C joins both notes and names the saving.

whyWrong.A: Oval red cells concern how the blood behaves once water is already lost, not how the animal avoids spending it on cooling.
whyWrong.B: Fast drinking is about replacing water after the fact, not reducing what is used.
whyWrong.D: Tolerating a large water loss is about withstanding dehydration rather than about the mechanism of keeping cool.

commonMistakes: Picking any note about water; the goal narrows it to water spent on temperature control.

whyCorrect: The goal is about how each canopy holds a jumper up, so the sentence has to name the physical force in each case. Choice A does: the ram-air canopy's inflated cells give it an aerofoil section that generates lift, while the older flat silk canopy produced only drag. That is a direct comparison of the supporting force, which is what was asked.

whyWrong.B: Adoption dates and fabric say nothing about the force that supports the jumper.
whyWrong.C: Slower descent and steerability are consequences of the aerofoil, not the explanation of how the canopy holds the jumper up.
whyWrong.D: This describes the old canopy alone, so no comparison is made and the mechanism is never named.

tips: When the goal asks how two things differ in mechanism, both mechanisms have to appear in the sentence.

whyCorrect: The sentence before establishes that the knot breaks its journey into three, and the underlined word picks up those pieces: each one ends at an estuary where the bird refuels. A portion of a journey ending at a stopping point is a leg, so choice B is the sense in use.

whyWrong.A: Scene of an event is a figurative sense of stage and does not fit something that ends at an estuary.
whyWrong.C: A raised platform is the literal theatrical sense and has nothing to do with migration.
whyWrong.D: Level of development would describe a phase in the bird's growth, but the passage is dividing a flight in space, not a life in time.

commonMistakes: Choosing a well-known meaning of the word instead of the one the preceding sentence has set up.

whyCorrect: Each colour in the basket comes from one specific preparation — boiled in the bark, stripped after boiling, stripped in spring — and no dye is involved. The bands of colour therefore preserve the history of how each bundle was treated, which is what a record does.

whyWrong.A: Concealment reverses the meaning: the colours reveal the preparation rather than hiding it.
whyWrong.C: Distortion would mean the colours misrepresent the treatment, but each colour follows directly from one method.
whyWrong.D: Forecast points forward in time, while the pattern reports what was already done to the rods.

tips: When the text says the pattern comes from the process itself rather than from something applied afterwards, the blank names evidence, not disguise.

whyCorrect: The passage says the salt is neither kept out nor pushed out; instead the plant takes up water so that the same salt is spread through a much larger volume of sap. Spreading a fixed quantity of solute through more solvent lowers its concentration, and the word for that is dilution.

whyWrong.B: Insulation would mean shielding the tissue from something, but the salt is already inside and is being spread rather than blocked.
whyWrong.C: Flotation is never suggested; the plant is rooted in mud, not buoyed up.
whyWrong.D: Concealment makes no sense of a chemical concentration problem.

tips: Same amount of salt, more water, means the concentration falls — name the process rather than the plant's appearance.

whyCorrect: The passage says the tension itself pulls the fibres into parallel layers and that this arrangement, not any coating, gives parchment its whiteness and hard writing surface. So drying under strain is not something done to a finished sheet — it is what makes the sheet what it is. Fundamental is the word for a step that constitutes the material.

whyWrong.A: Detrimental says the drying harms the parchment, when it produces its defining qualities.
whyWrong.B: Preliminary would make it a step that comes before the real process, but the sentence contrasts it with a finishing operation, not with a main one.
whyWrong.D: Incidental means unimportant or beside the point, the opposite of a step that creates the sheet's properties.

commonMistakes: Reading rather than a finishing operation as a hint that the step is early; the contrast is between constitutive and merely applied.

whyCorrect: The old method needed the miller to leave the stones and haul the tail pole by hand every time the wind shifted. The fantail described next turns the cap by itself whenever the wind strikes it sideways, so no one has to act at all. The blank names that change, and automatic is the only choice that captures a job now done without human intervention.

whyWrong.A: Communal would mean several people share the task, but the device removes the person rather than adding more.
whyWrong.B: Seasonal would tie the winding to a time of year, while the wind backs within a single afternoon.
whyWrong.C: Hazardous describes a risk, and nothing in the passage says the new arrangement is dangerous.

tips: When a passage replaces a person with a mechanism, the blank usually names the loss of manual effort.

whyCorrect: The opening sentence asserts the fact — a stone on old pasture sinks — without saying how. The underlined sentence supplies the how: worms bring soil up from depth as casts, and those casts wash down around the stone's edges so it is undermined grain by grain. Its function is to explain the mechanism behind that first assertion; Darwin's measurements come afterwards to give the rate.

whyWrong.A: The fifth of an inch a year figure appears in the following sentence, not the underlined one.
whyWrong.B: The underlined sentence raises no question of intent; the point about nobody burying the pavements is the closing sentence.
whyWrong.C: How Darwin collected and weighed the casts is described later; the underlined sentence describes what the worms do, not what the investigator did.

tips: An underlined sentence sitting between a claim and its evidence usually supplies the mechanism connecting them.

whyCorrect: The text explains a chemical change — clay particles repel one another in fresh water but clump once salt neutralises their charges — and then draws the geographic consequence: the mud drops out in the band where the two waters meet, and the dredgers return to those same few miles. The purpose is to account for that localisation.

whyWrong.A: Only one river's clay is discussed; no second river appears.
whyWrong.C: Dredgers are mentioned, but no equipment is described.
whyWrong.D: The text passes no judgement on whether dredging is worthwhile; it explains why it is repeatedly needed in one place.

commonMistakes: Taking the last clause about dredgers as the point; it is the illustration of the pattern the passage has just explained.

whyCorrect: The passage gives an advantage and a matching cost. The advantage is yield and sharpness: sixty or more blades from a fist-sized core, each edge a fracture surface a few molecules thick. The cost is durability: the edge dulls quickly and cannot be resharpened, only replaced. A main idea has to hold both halves together, which is what choice A does.

whyWrong.B: The last sentence says the opposite — an obsidian edge cannot be sharpened again.
whyWrong.C: Nothing about the availability or cost of cores to households appears in the text.
whyWrong.D: Sharpness is attributed to the fracture surface itself, not to the knapper's strength.

tips: When a passage names a benefit and then a limitation, expect the main idea to contain both.

whyCorrect: The passage describes a loop: waterlogging stops the dead moss rotting, the peat that builds up holds many times its own weight in water, and that stored water maintains the waterlogging which started the process. Because the bog carries its own wetness with it, it does not need a hollow, and the last sentence says it can climb a slope and cross a watershed. Choice B states both the self-sustaining mechanism and the consequence.

whyWrong.A: Peat holds water and releases it slowly, so drainage does not improve as it thickens.
whyWrong.C: The final sentence denies this: the bog is not confined to hollows.
whyWrong.D: No comparison of moss growth rates on slopes and level ground is made.

commonMistakes: Reading only the first sentence, where the wetness comes from the ground, and missing that the peat later supplies it.

whyCorrect: Beaudry's claim sets sediment supply against plant vigour, so the supporting finding must vary the sediment while leaving the plants alone. A dam cuts the sediment a river delivers, and the marshes below it fell relative to the tide over thirty years while marshes on a neighbouring undammed estuary rose. The outcome tracks sediment supply, which is exactly the claim.

whyWrong.A: Taller plants on rarely flooded ground describes a response to flooding rather than a cause of the marsh keeping its level.
whyWrong.B: Identical species and flowering times control for plant differences but show nothing about what determines the marsh's height.
whyWrong.C: That sediment settles more readily on a marsh than on bare flat compares two surfaces and does not test either explanation.

tips: An argument that X matters rather than Y is supported by a natural experiment in which X changes and Y does not.

whyCorrect: Ellery's claim has two parts: the mill's hours are set by the tide, and no improvement to the machinery can lengthen them. The quotation in choice D states both — the wheel turns only while the pond empties, and at neap tides that period is an hour shorter whatever gearing be put behind it. The gearing clause is what rules out a mechanical remedy.

whyWrong.A: Dressed millstones concern the condition of the plant and say nothing about working hours.
whyWrong.B: A price for new gates is a cost estimate, and it suggests improvement is possible rather than futile.
whyWrong.C: Where the corn comes from describes the mill's trade, not the limit on its running time.

tips: For a two-part claim, check that the quotation covers both parts, not just the more obvious one.

whyCorrect: The sentence needs the one field whose infiltration rate keeps up with the heaviest rain, which the passage puts at 20 millimetres an hour. Reading the infiltration column, Barn Close takes 6, Slade 9, Long Meadow 14 and Coldharbour 31 — only Coldharbour exceeds 20. Choice C names that field and gives the figure that makes it the only one.

whyWrong.A: Slade's 9 millimetres an hour is far below the 20 needed, and its bulk density is irrelevant to whether the rain soaks in.
whyWrong.B: Barn Close has the lowest rate of all at 6, so it is the least able to take the rainfall.
whyWrong.D: Long Meadow's 14 millimetres an hour is still below 20, so water would pond on it in the heaviest storms.

commonMistakes: Comparing the fields with each other and forgetting the 20 millimetre threshold the text supplies.

whyCorrect: Follow the two charges. Ammonium is positive and clings to the negatively charged clay and humus, so it stays put; but bacteria turn it into nitrate within days, and nitrate is negative and nothing in the soil holds it. Nitrogen applied in autumn therefore spends the whole wet winter as mobile nitrate, and drainage water carries it away.

whyWrong.B: The passage never says cool soil converts ammonium faster; conversion is described as quick in warm, moist ground, and faster conversion would in any case mean more loss, not less.
whyWrong.C: Holding in place is what ammonium does, and the conversion to nitrate happens within days, long before spring.
whyWrong.D: Lime and soil acidity are never mentioned in the passage.

tips: Track the charge: positive ions stick to soil particles, negative ones leave with the water.

whyCorrect: Each transplant isolates one limit. The high-marsh plant dies in the low marsh even with no competitor mentioned, so flooding alone stops it going down. The low-marsh plant grows perfectly well in the high marsh when its neighbour is cut away and is crowded out when it is not, so only competition stops it going up. Choice B assigns each boundary to the factor the experiments identify.

whyWrong.A: Removing the tide would not help the low-marsh plant, which is excluded from the high marsh by its neighbour rather than by water.
whyWrong.C: This denies competition, but the cut-away result shows competition is exactly what keeps the low-marsh plant out.
