whyWrong.D: Growth rate is never measured; the low-marsh plant is crowded out where the two meet, which if anything suggests the reverse.

commonMistakes: Assuming both zones are set by physical tolerance; the removal experiment is included precisely to separate the two causes.

whyCorrect: The subject is The longest rods and the verb is are kept back. Between them sits the appositive those over five feet, which renames the subject and is not essential to identifying it. A nonrestrictive appositive takes a comma on both sides, so commas after rods and after feet are both needed.

whyWrong.B: With no commas at all the appositive runs into the subject and the sentence reads as a single garbled noun phrase.
whyWrong.C: The opening comma is there but the closing one is missing, so the appositive is never shut before the verb.
whyWrong.D: The closing comma appears without the opening one, which is the same mismatch in reverse and also separates the subject from nothing.

tips: Appositive commas come in pairs — if you can delete the phrase and still have a sentence, both commas belong.

whyCorrect: The clause that stand along its side streets is restrictive: it tells you which compounds are meant, and without it The compounds would have no reference. A restrictive relative clause takes no commas, and the relative pronoun that is used only in restrictive clauses, so no punctuation belongs anywhere in the phrase.

whyWrong.A: Commas on both sides make the clause nonrestrictive, which conflicts with that and cuts the modifier loose from the noun it identifies.
whyWrong.B: Placing a comma after that splits the relative pronoun from its verb, which no rule permits.
whyWrong.D: A single comma before that both misuses the restrictive pronoun and separates the subject from its own modifier.

tips: That signals a restrictive clause, and restrictive clauses never take commas — which is the pronoun that can.

whyCorrect: The phrase a transformation that can take a year interrupts the sentence between the subordinate clause Only after it changes and the main clause does it grow the sucking disc. An interruption of this kind must be enclosed by a matching pair of marks, so a dash on each side is correct.

whyWrong.A: A comma opening and a dash closing is a mismatched pair.
whyWrong.B: A dash opening and a comma closing is the same mismatch reversed.
whyWrong.C: With no punctuation at all the appositive collides with the clause and reads as the object of changes.

commonMistakes: Choosing whichever single mark sounds right; parenthetical punctuation is decided by matching, not by pause length.

whyCorrect: It is nonetheless the order our own alphabet still runs in is a complete sentence, and the list of signs was already being recited and learned by heart as a sequence is another. With no conjunction between them, only a full stop among these options separates them correctly.

whyWrong.A: A comma between two independent clauses with no conjunction is a comma splice.
whyWrong.B: Without any mark the two clauses run together and the list of signs briefly reads as the object of runs in.
whyWrong.C: The commas around and are misplaced, isolating the conjunction from the clause it is meant to join.

tips: When the choices offer a comma and a period between two full clauses and no conjunction is present, the period is the safe one.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with the participial phrase Caught at the roost and weighed before release, so the noun immediately after the comma must be what was caught and weighed. Only the birds were caught, so the birds has to be the subject, and choice C also keeps the sentence in the active voice with a plain subject and verb.

whyWrong.A: It was found makes the placeholder it the thing caught at the roost, which nothing in the sentence supports.
whyWrong.B: This makes a gain the thing caught and weighed.
whyWrong.D: This makes eleven days the thing caught and weighed.

tips: After an opening participial phrase, read the first noun that follows the comma and ask whether it could have performed the action.

whyCorrect: The reference point is a past moment — By the time the roller plant opened in 1889 — and the decline of the stone-ground trade had started before it. An action completed before another past action takes the past perfect, so had already begun is required.

whyWrong.A: Has begun is present perfect and links the decline to the present, which clashes with the 1889 anchor.
whyWrong.B: Have is plural and disagrees with the singular subject the trade, besides being the wrong tense.
whyWrong.C: Having leaves the clause with no finite verb, turning the second half of the sentence into a fragment.

tips: By the time plus a past-tense event is the standard cue for the past perfect in the other clause.

whyCorrect: The subject is Each, which is singular; of the vents cut around the base of the clamp is a prepositional phrase and cannot govern the verb. The passage describes standing practice, so the singular present is is correct.

whyWrong.A: Were is plural and past, agreeing with vents rather than Each and shifting the sentence out of the present.
whyWrong.B: Have been is plural and present perfect, which describes completed action rather than the routine being described.
whyWrong.D: Are is plural and again agrees with the noun inside the prepositional phrase.

commonMistakes: Matching the verb to the closest noun; each, every and either are singular however many items follow them.

whyCorrect: The second sentence establishes that nothing rolled or was carried by animal on these roads — every load moved on a person's back. The third says the roads were nevertheless built wide, level and hard enough for traffic that did not exist. Building to a standard the actual traffic never required runs against what the preceding sentence would lead you to expect, so a concessive transition is needed.

whyWrong.B: Consequently would make the heavy road specification a result of there being no vehicles, which is the reverse of the surprise the sentence records.
whyWrong.C: Likewise marks a parallel case, and no second case is offered.
whyWrong.D: That is introduces a restatement, but the third sentence adds a new and contrary fact about how the roads were built.

tips: Watch for a detail that is more than the situation calls for — that mismatch is signalled with a concession.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences establish that peat comes out two-thirds water, will not burn wet, and has to be stacked, turned twice and left until it rings under the hand. The sentence after the blank draws the conclusion those facts add up to: free fuel that costs a summer of labour. A conclusion drawn from what precedes takes Therefore.

whyWrong.A: However would set the conclusion against the preceding description, but it follows directly from it.
whyWrong.B: Similarly requires a second parallel case, and none is given.
whyWrong.C: For instance would make the closing sentence an example of the drying routine rather than the summary it is.

commonMistakes: Being pulled toward a contrast word by the paradox inside the final sentence; the contrast is between buying and working, not between this sentence and the last.

whyCorrect: The first sentence makes a general claim: neither temperature nor moisture predicts a soil's behaviour by itself. The second gives a specific case where the warmer soil gives off less carbon dioxide because it is saturated and its organisms are short of oxygen. A concrete instance illustrating a general claim takes For example.

whyWrong.A: As a result would make the particular comparison a consequence of the general claim rather than evidence for it.
whyWrong.B: In conclusion signals a summing up, but the second sentence introduces new detail rather than closing the discussion.
whyWrong.D: However requires opposition, and the example confirms the claim that one factor alone is not enough.

tips: A general statement followed by one specific case is almost always an example, not a consequence.

whyCorrect: The goal asks how a single standard reached an individual trader, so the sentence has to follow the chain all the way down. Choice D does: one London set, copies sent to the market towns, officers comparing each trader's measure against the copy, and a stamp on the ones that matched. Every link from the central standard to the trader's own vessel is present.

whyWrong.A: Sending standards to the towns covers only the middle of the chain and never reaches the trader.
whyWrong.B: Variation between towns is the problem being solved, not the mechanism that solved it.
whyWrong.C: The copying from a London set is one link and stops short of the market.

tips: For a how-did-it-reach question, check that the sentence runs from the source all the way to the endpoint named in the goal.

whyCorrect: The phrase returning to the rock it came from needs a round trip, so the sentence must show the carbon dioxide leaving and coming back. Choice B has both: burning drives it out of the limestone, the set takes it back from the air, and the result is the same carbonate the stone was made of. That identity of starting and finishing material is what makes the description apt.

whyWrong.A: This gives only the outward half of the cycle, so nothing returns.
whyWrong.C: Continued hardening describes how long the process runs, not what the material becomes.
whyWrong.D: Slaking is an intermediate step and does not involve carbon dioxide at all.

commonMistakes: Choosing a note that is chemically true but describes only one direction of a two-way change.

whyCorrect: The goal calls for a comparison of precision, so the sentence must state what the Maya system does and what the neighbouring systems do. Choice C supplies the mechanism — a continuous day count from one fixed point that never restarts with a new ruler, allowing a date to the individual day — and sets it against dating by reign. Only that pairing explains the difference in precision.

whyWrong.A: The decades of scholarly work concern modern correlation with the European calendar, not the precision of the original dates.
whyWrong.B: The fixed starting point is half the mechanism and no comparison is drawn.
whyWrong.D: Dating by reign gives only the comparison case with nothing to compare it to.

tips: A why-is-X-more-precise question needs both systems in the sentence, and the feature that separates them.

whyCorrect: The passage describes building in fixed steps: courses about half a metre high, each of which must dry and carry its own weight before the next goes on. The wall can only rise a stage at a time over a season, and incremental is the word for work that proceeds in successive small additions.

whyWrong.B: Collaborative concerns how many people work on the wall, which the passage never raises.
whyWrong.C: Improvised would mean unplanned, but the method described is a fixed and unhurried sequence.
whyWrong.D: Cost is never mentioned; the constraint described is time.

tips: The blank has to follow from the sentence right before it — here that sentence is about time and stages, not money or teamwork.

whyCorrect: The sentence structure is not that it lasts but that it is so easily _____, so the blank must name a virtue that compensates for a short life. The passage supplies it directly: a fresh coat costs only the lime and a morning's work. Something cheap and quick to reapply is easily repeated, and that is what makes the short life unimportant.

whyWrong.A: Imitated would concern other people copying the finish, which has nothing to do with the wall's durability.
whyWrong.C: Tinting is never mentioned; the passage discusses breathability and cost.
whyWrong.D: Removal is not the point — nothing in the passage treats getting the limewash off as a benefit.

commonMistakes: Ignoring the not that it lasts but frame, which requires a virtue that answers the lack of durability.

whyCorrect: The passage says rain runs down the outside of the stems and off the eaves without penetrating more than a few centimetres, and that pitch matters because a shallow roof lets water travel along the stems instead of down them. The roof works by getting water off the surface quickly, which is what shedding means, and the contrast with blocking confirms it.

whyWrong.A: Absorbing is the opposite of what the text describes: water barely enters the coat at all.
whyWrong.B: Storing would mean holding the water, which is precisely the failure a shallow pitch causes.
whyWrong.C: Filtering implies water passes through while something is strained out, but the water is meant not to pass through.

tips: Read the contrast at the end of the sentence — rather than by blocking tells you the answer is a way of moving water, not stopping it.

whyCorrect: The middle sentence gives the reason for the slowness: hurrying fixes the outer faces before the liquor has penetrated the middle, and the leather then cracks along the fold. The slow sequence therefore serves a purpose the tanner understood, which is what deliberate says, and the rather than clause confirms the contrast is with backwardness.

whyWrong.A: Seasonal would tie the pace to a time of year, but the constraint is how long the liquor takes to reach the centre of the hide.
whyWrong.C: Customary makes the slowness a matter of habit, which is close to the very charge — an unimproved industry — that the sentence rejects.
whyWrong.D: Unrecorded concerns documentation and has no bearing on why the process took a year.

tips: When a sentence ends rather than a mark of backwardness, the blank must assert purpose.

whyCorrect: The sentence describes the kiln being fed continuously: quicklime is drawn off at the grate and another one is added at the top as the column settles. What is added at the top is another load of coal and limestone, so the word names a quantity of material put in at one time.

whyWrong.A: A fee is the commercial sense and nothing is being paid for here.
whyWrong.B: A duty assigned would be a responsibility, but the thing added goes into the shaft of a kiln.
whyWrong.D: An accusation is the legal sense and has no place in a description of loading a kiln.

tips: Substitute each meaning into the sentence — only one can be added at the top of a kiln.

whyCorrect: The first sentence gives the old method's fault: stones crush everything at once, the germ oil is smeared through the meal and the flour goes rancid. The last sentence lists the new flour's qualities — white, keeps for months, travels anywhere. The underlined sentence sits between them and describes the mechanism, shearing each grain so bran and germ come off in siftable flakes, which is what produces those qualities.

whyWrong.B: Nothing is conceded to stone-ground flour; the first sentence gives only its drawback.
whyWrong.C: The passage takes the oil in the germ as given and never explains why it is there.
whyWrong.D: The timing of the country mills' decline is stated in the final sentence, not the underlined one.

tips: A sentence placed between a problem and a set of results usually functions as the mechanism that links them.

whyCorrect: The underlined sentence describes the construction in detail: crossed pairs of pegs driven into the swamp, a rail dropped into each crossing, planks pegged onto the rail. The two sentences after it draw out what that arrangement achieved — nothing rested on the surface, and the walkway carried people over ground that would not hold a standing adult. So its function is to lay out the structure whose purpose the rest of the text explains.

whyWrong.A: The date of about 3800 BCE is given in the first sentence, not the underlined one.
whyWrong.B: Why the timbers survived in peat is never discussed anywhere in the text.
whyWrong.C: No later roads are mentioned, so no comparison is drawn.

commonMistakes: Answering with what the sentence is about rather than what job it does for the sentences around it.

whyCorrect: The passage explains the principle — each picture stands for the sound that opens the word naming it, so the ox head writes that first sound — and then gives the payoff: twenty-odd signs where a word-by-word system needed several hundred, short enough for non-scribes to learn in days. The main idea joins that device to the drastic reduction in signs.

whyWrong.A: The passage says the opposite, that twenty-odd signs covered the language.
whyWrong.C: Ease of drawing is never mentioned; the signs are chosen for the words they name.
whyWrong.D: No resistance by scribes appears in the text.

tips: When a text explains a device and then its consequence, the main idea usually names both.

whyCorrect: The passage defines the acre as a day's ploughing rather than a fixed area, notes that its size therefore varied with the soil, and then splits the consequences: it told the farmer exactly how long a field would take, and told a distant purchaser nothing about how much ground he was getting. Choice C states that split — precise about labour, vague about area.

whyWrong.A: Horses and the abandonment of the unit are never mentioned.
whyWrong.B: No preference of farmers for one soil is expressed; the soils only illustrate the variation in size.
whyWrong.D: Productivity is not compared; the same day's work simply covers less clay than loam, which is the definition rather than a judgement of the ploughman.

commonMistakes: Reading the clay-versus-loam sentence as the point; it is an illustration of the unit's variability.

whyCorrect: The standard is 35.2 litres, so take each town's difference from it: Barrowden 37.7 is 2.5 over, Chettle 33.1 is 2.1 under, Denton 35.2 is exact, Elsdon 40.0 is 4.8 over. The largest gap by far is Elsdon's, and choice D names that town with the correct difference.

whyWrong.A: Chettle's 2.1 litres is the smallest of the three deviations, not the largest.
whyWrong.B: Barrowden's 2.5 litres is larger than Chettle's but only about half Elsdon's.
whyWrong.C: Denton matched the standard exactly, so it is the fourth town — the one that did not differ at all.

tips: Compute every difference from the standard before choosing; the largest raw capacity is not automatically the largest deviation, though here it is.

whyCorrect: Achebe's claim is that living organisms, not chemistry, do the suppressing. Heating kills organisms while leaving the soil's chemistry largely intact, and the finding says heating destroys the suppression. The second half is what clinches it: adding one part of untreated soil to fifty parts of heated soil brings the suppression back, which is behaviour characteristic of something that multiplies — a living population — rather than a chemical present at a fixed concentration.

whyWrong.B: More organic matter is consistent with either explanation, since organic matter alters chemistry as well as supporting organisms.
whyWrong.C: Seasonal severity describes the disease, not the mechanism of suppression.
whyWrong.D: A wide geographic spread shows the phenomenon is common but says nothing about its cause.

tips: A tiny inoculum restoring a lost property is the classic signature of a living agent.

whyCorrect: Rask's claim is that the notebook records its author convincing himself the piles were structural. The quotation has to show reasoning, not just observation, and choice A does: it notes the regular four-abreast spacing, rules out flood as an explanation, and states the conclusion he draws — footings of something raised above the water. That is the moment of persuasion Rask describes.

whyWrong.B: The depth of the ditch and the placing of the spoil are routine site notes with no interpretation.
whyWrong.C: The landowner's permission concerns access to the field, not the nature of the piles.
whyWrong.D: Sawing two piles and sending them to a museum records an action taken, not the reasoning behind a conclusion.

commonMistakes: Picking a quotation that mentions the piles; the claim is about interpretation, so the quotation must contain an inference.

whyCorrect: The passage gives one rule and only one: the figures always face towards the start of the line, so a row of leftward-looking owls is read from the left. What a first-time reader gains from that rule is the ability to find the beginning of each line. Choice D states exactly that and nothing more.

whyWrong.A: Reading direction is not translation; the rule says nothing about what the signs mean.
whyWrong.B: Direction varies within a single wall, so it cannot date anything.
whyWrong.C: Who the inscription honours is a matter of content, which the facing rule does not touch.

commonMistakes: Over-extending a narrow rule; the passage supports a conclusion about direction only.

whyCorrect: The passage defines the test: a section brown throughout means the liquor has done its work, and a pale line down the middle is an untanned core. A pale line therefore says the tannin has not yet reached the centre, and since tannin enters slowly from both faces, the remedy is more time in the pits. Choice C reads the sign correctly and draws the action that follows from it.

whyWrong.A: The age of the animal is never mentioned; the test reports how far the liquor has penetrated.
whyWrong.B: The strip is cut from the edge as the standard method, so a pale line is a result, not evidence of bad sampling.
whyWrong.D: Scorching by strong liquor is not described anywhere; the pale core means too little tannin inside, not too much outside.

tips: For a diagnostic test, match the observation to the definition the passage gives, then act on it.

whyCorrect: Four miles of clean gravel names the Kirkby reach, and which had held no spawning fish since the weir was raised adds information about it without narrowing which gravel is meant. A nonrestrictive relative clause introduced by which is attached with a comma.

whyWrong.A: A colon introduces a naming or explaining element, not a relative clause beginning with which.
whyWrong.C: Omitting the comma makes the clause restrictive, which is wrong both because which is used and because the gravel has already been identified.
whyWrong.D: A semicolon must be followed by an independent clause, and which had held no spawning fish cannot stand alone.

tips: A which clause adding detail to an already identified noun takes a comma, every time.

whyCorrect: The core of the sentence is The hides are stiff enough to stand on edge, with the restrictive clause that come out of the strongest liquor identifying which hides. Nothing here is parenthetical, so no punctuation belongs between the subject and its verb or between the verb and its complement.

whyWrong.A: The comma after are cuts the verb off from the adjective completing it.
whyWrong.B: This adds two commas, one separating the subject from its verb and one separating the verb from its complement.
whyWrong.D: A single comma after liquor still splits the subject The hides that come out of the strongest liquor from the verb are.

commonMistakes: Inserting a comma wherever a long subject ends; a subject is never separated from its verb by a single comma.

whyCorrect: Their branching pattern settles the one question that matters to every plant growing on the marsh is a complete sentence, and what follows states what that question is. A colon after a complete clause is the mark that introduces the thing the clause has been pointing at.

whyWrong.A: A semicolon needs an independent clause after it, and how long each patch of ground lies under salt water is a noun clause, not a sentence.
whyWrong.C: A comma is too weak to introduce the announced question and leaves the how clause dangling.
whyWrong.D: With no punctuation the how clause reads as a modifier of marsh, which garbles the sense.

tips: A clause that promises a question, a reason or a list is nearly always followed by a colon.

whyCorrect: Because the same water carries the colour down with it is a subordinate clause opening the sentence, and a podzol shows a bleached grey band lying directly above a rust-coloured one is the main clause. An introductory subordinate clause is followed by a comma.

whyWrong.B: With no comma the boundary is unmarked and a podzol briefly reads as part of the Because clause.
whyWrong.C: A semicolon requires an independent clause on its left, and a clause beginning with Because is not one.
whyWrong.D: A colon likewise requires a complete clause before it.

tips: Any sentence opening with Because needs a comma at the point where the main clause starts.

whyCorrect: The pronoun is the second object of the preposition by: written jointly by the field director and her. Objects of prepositions take the objective form, and the test is to drop the other noun — written by her is right, written by she is not.

whyWrong.B: She is the subject form and cannot follow a preposition.
whyWrong.C: Hers is a possessive pronoun and would mean something belonging to her, not the person herself.
whyWrong.D: Herself is reflexive and needs a matching subject earlier in the clause; the subject here is the report.

tips: Delete the other half of the compound and read it aloud — the correct case becomes obvious.

whyCorrect: Ever since that winter marks a period running from a point in the past up to now, and the district is still being drained by the diesel pumps. A state that began in the past and continues into the present takes the present perfect, has been kept.

whyWrong.A: Is kept describes the present alone and does not cover the stretch of time since 1938 that ever since requires.
whyWrong.B: Was kept places the arrangement wholly in the past, implying it has ended.
whyWrong.C: Had been kept is the past perfect, which needs a later past reference point; there is none here.

tips: Since or ever since plus a past date is the standard cue for the present perfect.

whyCorrect: The batch belongs to the masons the previous sentence introduced, and there is more than one of them. A plural noun already ending in s takes an apostrophe after the s, giving The masons' first batch.

whyWrong.A: Masons's adds a second s to a plural that already ends in one, which standard usage does not do.
whyWrong.C: The mason's is singular and contradicts the masons described in the sentence before.
whyWrong.D: The masons with no apostrophe is a plain plural, leaving first batch with no grammatical connection to it.

tips: Work out the number of owners from the previous sentence, then place the apostrophe.

whyCorrect: The passage establishes that the gizzard shrinks before a long flight and takes several days to rebuild, so on arrival the bird has no organ capable of grinding shells. Eating soft-bodied worms first is the direct consequence of that. A result marker is needed, and Accordingly is the only one offered.

whyWrong.A: Even so concedes something against expectation, but soft food is exactly what a shrunken gizzard would predict.
whyWrong.B: By contrast requires an opposition, and the last sentence follows from the preceding ones.
whyWrong.C: Specifically would narrow a claim just made, but the last sentence introduces new behaviour rather than refining the gizzard description.

commonMistakes: Reading a change of subject from the organ to the diet as a contrast; it is a consequence.

whyCorrect: Mole draining is described as splitting the clay into fissures that lead down to the pipe. The sentence after the blank states the outcome — water reaches the pipe by a route the soil could not have provided itself. That is the effect of the operation just described, so a result transition is required.

whyWrong.A: Nonetheless would set the outcome against the moling, when the outcome is what moling achieves.
whyWrong.B: By comparison introduces a contrast between two cases, and only one method is described here.
whyWrong.C: For instance would make the water's route an example of pulling a mole through clay rather than its result.

tips: An operation described, then what it achieves, is cause and effect.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences favour reed: it stands upright and lasts sixty years against straw's twenty-five. The third gives straw's compensating advantages — cheaper to lay, patchable in a morning. Granting a benefit to the option that looked worse is a concession, which is what Even so marks.

whyWrong.A: Similarly would present the third sentence as agreeing with the durability comparison, but it points the other way.
whyWrong.B: In particular narrows a preceding general claim, and the third sentence introduces new grounds rather than detail on the old ones.
whyWrong.D: Therefore would make straw's cheapness a consequence of its shorter life, which the passage does not claim.

tips: When a passage rates two options and then names an advantage of the weaker one, expect a concession.

whyCorrect: The goal asks how one piece of ground yields two things at once, so the sentence must contain both products and the feature that lets them coexist. Choice D has all three: the cut is made above browsing height, so the regrowth survives, and the ground carries grazing animals and a wood crop together.

whyWrong.A: Longevity of the tree is a separate benefit and does not explain how two products share the ground.
whyWrong.B: The definition of a pollard gives the method but never mentions the grazing animals it makes room for.
whyWrong.C: The uses of the poles describe one product only.

tips: Count the elements the goal names — here two yields plus the reason they can share the ground — and check the choice contains them all.

whyCorrect: The goal asks why the ridge is treated separately, which needs two things: a reason it must be renewed on its own schedule and a reason it can be. Choice A gives both — the ridge wears out several times during the life of the coat, and it can be stripped without disturbing the coat beneath — and adds that the job takes only a few days.

whyWrong.B: The quantity of sedge is a cost detail and explains nothing about the separate treatment.
whyWrong.C: Heavier weathering explains why the ridge wears faster but not why it can be replaced by itself.
whyWrong.D: The renewal interval alone gives no comparison with the coat and no mechanism.

commonMistakes: Settling for the note that gives the cause of wear; the question also needs what makes separate renewal possible.

whyCorrect: The goal asks why the expense of a leat is worth it, so the sentence has to connect the leat to a payoff. Choice C does: carrying water along the contour delivers it at the height an overshot wheel requires, and an overshot wheel gives about twice the power of an undershot one on the same flow. The doubled power is what justifies the digging.

whyWrong.A: This says what a leat does but names no benefit, so no expense is justified.
whyWrong.B: The undershot wheel's mechanism is background with no leat involved.
whyWrong.D: The overshot wheel's mechanism explains how it works but not why the extra construction pays.

tips: A why-spend-the-money question needs the benefit stated, not just the thing being bought.

whyCorrect: The passage says the bar was not a description of a length but the length itself, that every yard in the kingdom descended from it, and that a dispute could be settled by laying a measure alongside it. That is the definition of a reference object against which other things are checked, which is choice C.

whyWrong.A: A level of quality expected is the everyday sense, but the passage describes a physical bar kept at the Exchequer.
whyWrong.B: A usual way of proceeding is the sense in standard practice and does not fit something you lay a yard beside.
whyWrong.D: A flag carried in procession is a real sense of the word and is exactly the kind of familiar meaning that does not fit here.

tips: When the text says a thing is not a description of X but X itself, it is describing a physical reference object.

whyCorrect: Every feature of the dressing is given a job: the furrow edges cut the grain instead of crushing it, and the furrows carry meal and cooling air out to the rim. The last clause adds the proof — a smooth stone heats and spoils the flour. Since the pattern exists entirely to do work, functional is the precise word.

whyWrong.B: Traditional would attribute the pattern to inherited practice, but the passage gives mechanical reasons for every part of it.
whyWrong.C: Ornamental is contradicted by the whole passage, which shows the pattern doing the grinding.
whyWrong.D: Provisional would mean temporary, and nothing suggests the dressing is a stopgap.

tips: When each feature is explained by what it does, the blank names purpose, not custom or decoration.

whyCorrect: The first sentence says elvers cannot cross a smooth vertical face with water sheeting down it, so before the fitting the weir stopped them completely. The bristle channel gives them purchase all the way up, and the sentence contrasts what the barrier had been with merely inconvenient. Only impassable names the total block that merely inconvenient is set against.

whyWrong.A: Unlawful concerns regulation, and the obstacle described is physical.
whyWrong.B: Expensive would describe a cost to someone, but the barrier's effect on elvers is that they cannot climb it.
whyWrong.C: Invisible has no bearing on whether the elvers can get up the face.

tips: The word in the blank has to be the extreme that merely inconvenient softens.

whyCorrect: The passage sets narrow limits on both sides: without air the fire dies and the stack is wasted, with too much air the wood burns to ash instead of charring. The burner's whole night is spent opening one vent and stopping another to hold the fire just short of proper combustion. Keeping it starved names that deliberate restriction of air.

whyWrong.B: Hidden describes concealment, but the earth covering exists to limit air, not to conceal the fire.
whyWrong.C: Sheltered would mean protecting the fire from outside conditions, when the work described is restricting its air supply.
whyWrong.D: Portable is irrelevant to a stack built on the ground and burned in place.

commonMistakes: Reading the earth covering as protection; it is there to control how much air gets in.

whyCorrect: Each layer of twist is trying to unwind and is held by the layer around it twisting the other way, so the forces are opposed and balanced. That balance is why the rope holds along its length but frays once cut and the opposition is released. Equilibrium is the word for opposed forces in balance.

whyWrong.A: Sequence describes order, and the layers are not arranged in time but pulling against one another.
whyWrong.B: In reserve would mean held back for later use, but the twists are acting on each other continuously.
whyWrong.D: In suspension describes something held up or dispersed in a fluid and does not name balanced opposing forces.

tips: Two forces pulling in opposite directions and cancelling is equilibrium, whatever the material.

whyCorrect: The text lines up three facts: bill lengths range from two to twelve centimetres, prey is layered by depth in the mud, and the diet records show almost no overlap between shortest and longest bills. Together they explain how six species can feed on the same flat at the same tide without taking the same food.

whyWrong.B: No aggression or displacement is described; the species feed simultaneously.
whyWrong.C: Burrow construction is never discussed, only the depths at which animals lie.
whyWrong.D: Numbers of each species are not given, so no ranking is established.

commonMistakes: Turning a description of coexistence into a story about competition; the passage reports separation, not conflict.

whyCorrect: The underlined sentence describes how a corbelled vault is built — each course set further out until a capstone closes the gap. Everything after it follows from that method: no sideways load path, so very thick walls, so rooms that are narrow, tall and dark, and a steep cost for widening. Its function is to state the construction whose consequences the rest of the text works out.

whyWrong.A: The capstone is mentioned, but nothing is said about its weight relative to other stones.
whyWrong.B: The tallness of the rooms comes later and as a consequence, not as a figure given in the underlined sentence.
whyWrong.D: No true arch or other tradition is brought in for comparison.

tips: If everything after the underlined sentence is a consequence of it, its function is to state the premise.

whyCorrect: The passage argues that lime mortar's weakness is deliberate: cracks form along the joints, and joints are the one part of a wall a mason can rake out and replace. Cement is stronger and stiffer, so in soft brickwork the crack goes through the brick instead, which cannot be repaired that way. Choice D holds the principle and the practical warning together.

whyWrong.A: The passage says cement is stronger and stiffer; the point is where the crack goes, not which mortar cracks more.
whyWrong.B: Replacing the bricks is never suggested; the argument is about which mortar to use with soft brick.
whyWrong.C: Cost is not mentioned anywhere in the text.

tips: When a text says a weakness is the point of something, the main idea will be about where damage is directed, not about strength.

whyCorrect: The text sets out two constructions — a coiled wall built by sewing a spiral bundle, and a woven wall built by threading fine rods through upright stouter ones — and then pairs each with what it demands: a needle and little strength for the first, rods that bend without cracking and a maker who can hold them under strain for the second. The main idea is that link between how the wall is built and what it requires.

whyWrong.A: Grass and straw belong to the coiled method only; the woven method uses rods.
whyWrong.B: No order of learning is discussed anywhere.
whyWrong.D: Strength and lifespan of the finished baskets are never compared.

commonMistakes: Stopping at the description of the two methods; the last sentence extends the idea to material and tools, and the main idea has to cover it.

whyCorrect: Sørensen's claim names a specific sense, so the supporting finding has to take that sense away and show the behaviour collapse. Plugging the nostrils does exactly that: those fish turned into the two branches at random, while fish from the same run with their sense of smell intact went overwhelmingly into their natal branch. Removing the smell removes the correct choosing, which is what implicates smell.

whyWrong.A: Time spent in fresh water before migrating allows for learning but shows nothing about what sense is used on the return.
whyWrong.B: A temperature difference between branches offers a rival cue rather than support for smell.
whyWrong.D: Return numbers varying with autumn flow concerns how many fish come back, not how they navigate.

tips: To show a particular sense is responsible, look for the experiment that blocks it and watches the behaviour fail.

whyCorrect: Larkin's claim ranks two inputs: bark constrained output, hides did not. The quotation in choice B does both jobs in one sentence — hides could be had from Cork whenever they sent for them, and it is the bark that settles how many pits they dare lay down. That is the firm itself naming bark as the binding constraint.

whyWrong.A: Hiring beam house men concerns labour, a third input the claim does not involve.
whyWrong.C: The dimensions and date of new pits describe the plant, not what limited its use.
whyWrong.D: The price of sole leather is about the market for the output, not the supply of either input.

commonMistakes: Choosing a quotation that mentions one of the two inputs; the claim is comparative, so the quotation must rank them.

whyCorrect: The sentence asks for the largest gain, which means subtracting arrival mass from departure mass at each site: Dornoch 205 minus 130 is 75 grams, Solway 196 minus 128 is 68, Ribble 171 minus 126 is 45, Wash 188 minus 133 is 55. Dornoch's 75 grams is the biggest, and choice B names it with both figures.

whyWrong.A: The Solway's 196 grams is a departure mass, not a gain, and its gain of 68 grams is second.
whyWrong.C: The Wash's arrival mass is the highest of the four, but a high starting point is not a large gain; its gain was 55 grams.
whyWrong.D: The Ribble's gain of 45 grams is the smallest in the table.

tips: When a sentence asks for a gain or a change, compute the difference for every row before choosing — the largest single figure is rarely the answer.

whyCorrect: Two facts have to be combined. The flight was eight days with no stop, and before leaving the bird had doubled its lean weight in fat while its digestive organs shrank to a fraction of their size. A bird that cannot digest cannot refuel in flight, so everything it burned over those eight days had to be on board at departure.

whyWrong.A: Winds are never mentioned, and nothing in the observations bears on whether the flight was wind-assisted.
whyWrong.C: Feeding at sea is ruled out by the shrunken digestive organs and by the record of no stop.
whyWrong.D: No comparison of speeds is made, and the fat is fuel for the crossing rather than a handicap the passage measures.

tips: An inference question with two observations usually wants the conclusion that needs both of them.

whyCorrect: The column rests on the clay below the peat and has not moved since 1851, when its top was level with the field. Its top now stands more than three metres proud, and the passage explains that drained peat shrinks and wastes away. The fixed column therefore measures how far the ground surface has dropped.

whyWrong.B: The column is the fixed reference; nothing suggests the clay rose, and the passage supplies a mechanism for the peat falling instead.
whyWrong.C: No drain or water level is mentioned, and the column records the position of the ground surface.
whyWrong.D: A three-metre gap shows how much wasting has happened, not that it has stopped.

commonMistakes: Reading the column as having risen; it is the only thing in the scene that has not moved.

whyCorrect: Both halves are complete sentences, and however is a conjunctive adverb, not a coordinating conjunction, so it cannot join them by itself. Two independent clauses linked by however take a semicolon before it and a comma after it.

whyWrong.B: A comma before however leaves two independent clauses joined by a comma, which is a comma splice.
whyWrong.C: With no mark before however the clauses simply run together.
whyWrong.D: A colon announces an explanation or a list rather than a contrast, and the missing comma after however compounds the error.

tips: However, therefore and moreover need a semicolon in front of them when a full clause stands on each side.

whyCorrect: The frames were reared one after another and pegged together along the length of the building first is one independent clause, and the walls were built around them afterwards and carry no part of the roof at all is another. When and joins two full clauses, a comma goes before it.

whyWrong.A: The comma after and is misplaced, cutting the conjunction off from the clause it introduces.
whyWrong.C: With no comma the boundary between the two clauses is unmarked and the walls momentarily reads as another object of pegged together.
whyWrong.D: A comma with no conjunction between two independent clauses is a comma splice.

tips: Check whether what follows and has its own subject and verb; if it does, put a comma before the and.

whyCorrect: The gear does the one thing no earlier sail could do is a complete clause that promises to name that one thing, and the words after the blank supply it. A colon after a complete clause is the mark that makes that introduction, and what follows it here is itself a full clause explaining the promise.

whyWrong.A: A comma between do and it spills joins two independent clauses without a conjunction, which is a comma splice.
whyWrong.B: With no punctuation at all the two clauses run together.
whyWrong.C: A colon immediately followed by and is not a valid construction.

commonMistakes: Thinking a colon must be followed by a list or a phrase; it can introduce a full clause that delivers what the first clause promised.

whyCorrect: A mason working to a lime specification plans for the delay and slakes the lime long before the wall is begun is a complete sentence, and mortar mixed the same week is gritty, harsh under the trowel and slow to set is another. Two independent clauses with no coordinating conjunction between them are joined by a semicolon.

whyWrong.A: With nothing between them the clauses run together and begun mortar reads as a single phrase.
whyWrong.B: A colon followed by and is not a construction English uses.
whyWrong.D: A comma between two independent clauses without a conjunction is a comma splice.

tips: Cover the blank and read each side alone — two complete sentences and no conjunction means a semicolon.

whyCorrect: The sentence opens with the participial phrase Bent up out of the finished base and held under strain, so the noun straight after the comma has to be the thing bent and held. Those are the stakes, and choice A puts them in subject position with a plain active verb.

whyWrong.B: This makes the shape the thing bent up and held under strain, which is a dangling modifier.
whyWrong.C: There is a shape puts a placeholder in subject position, so nothing in the clause was bent up out of the base.
whyWrong.D: The subject becomes taking the shape, a gerund phrase, which again cannot be what was bent and held.

commonMistakes: Choosing by meaning rather than by what noun follows the comma; the opening phrase always describes that noun.

whyCorrect: The subject is The number, which is singular; of distinct local bushels reported to it in 1826 is a modifier standing between the subject and the verb. The sentence describes the 1826 return, a completed past event, so the singular past was is correct.

whyWrong.A: Are is plural and present, agreeing with bushels rather than with the number.
whyWrong.C: Were is plural and again takes its agreement from the noun inside the modifier.
whyWrong.D: Have been is plural and present perfect, which does not fit a fixed historical count.

tips: The number of is singular; a number of is plural — the article decides it.

whyCorrect: The word needed is a possessive attached to any pass, a singular noun, so it must be the singular possessive its. Its has no apostrophe; the apostrophe form it's is the contraction of it is.

whyWrong.A: Their is plural and does not agree with the singular any pass.
whyWrong.B: They're is the contraction of they are, which is both plural and a verb where a possessive is needed.
whyWrong.D: It's means it is, so the sentence would read has it is trickle of water restored.

tips: Expand the apostrophe form: if it is does not fit, the word you want is its.

whyCorrect: The first two sentences give two directions actually used — right to left, and alternating line by line. The sentence after the blank draws the conclusion those examples add up to: left to right was for a long time just one option among several. A summing-up of the preceding evidence takes In short.

whyWrong.A: Nevertheless marks a concession, but the conclusion follows straight from the examples rather than resisting them.
whyWrong.C: By contrast needs an opposition, and the final sentence generalizes over the earlier ones instead of opposing them.
whyWrong.D: For example would make the closing sentence a further instance, when it is the point the instances support.

tips: Two or more examples followed by the claim they demonstrate is a summary, not a contrast.

whyCorrect: Sole leather is described as thick and firm so it wears rather than stretches; upper leather is curried with oils and tallow until it is soft enough to fold at every step. The two are opposite in treatment and in the property aimed for, so a contrast transition is needed.

whyWrong.B: Accordingly would make the soft upper a consequence of the firm sole, which the passage does not claim.
whyWrong.C: In addition presents the second fact as a further similar point, ignoring that it is the opposite treatment.
whyWrong.D: In other words signals a restatement, but nothing in the second sentence repeats the first.

tips: Two materials described with opposite properties for opposite jobs is the standard contrast setup.

whyCorrect: Charring removes well over half the weight and leaves a fuel that burns hotter, so a horseload of charcoal carries far more usable heat than a horseload of wood. Burning the wood where it grew and carrying out only the charcoal is the direct consequence of that weight loss, so a result transition is required.

whyWrong.A: Meanwhile marks simultaneity, and the second sentence is caused by the first rather than merely concurrent with it.
whyWrong.C: Nevertheless would set the practice against the weight loss, when the weight loss is precisely why the practice made sense.
whyWrong.D: For example would make the transport arrangement an instance of losing weight in charring, which it is not.

commonMistakes: Treating the weight loss as a drawback; for transport it is exactly the advantage.

whyCorrect: The goal asks what blocking the ditches changes about the bog's behaviour, so the sentence needs the intervention and a measured change. Choice A gives both: the water table comes back to within a few centimetres of the surface, and gas measurements then record far less carbon dioxide leaving the ground. That is the change in what the bog does.

whyWrong.B: Surface loss on a drained field describes the condition before the intervention.
whyWrong.C: The waterlogging requirement is background chemistry with no ditch blocking in it.
whyWrong.D: The return of sphagnum is a real change but describes what grows on the site rather than what the ground does, and it omits the blocking that caused it.

tips: An explain-the-change question needs the action and the measured outcome in the same sentence.

whyCorrect: To show parchment is not leather you need the defining difference and a consequence that follows from it. Choice B supplies both: parchment is dried under tension with no tannin, so wetting relaxes and cockles it, while a tanned hide dries flat and unchanged. The behaviour on wetting is the test that separates the two materials.

whyWrong.A: A shared raw material is what makes the two easy to confuse, so it argues the wrong way.
whyWrong.C: Liming and scraping describe part of the process but never contrast parchment with tanned leather.
whyWrong.D: The permanence of tanning describes leather alone and leaves parchment unmentioned.

commonMistakes: Naming only the absence of tannin; the strongest answer also shows the difference in how the two materials behave.

whyCorrect: The goal is about how the breach changed the life of the site, so the sentence must connect the tide's return to living things. Choice A does: glasswort colonised the bare mud within two seasons and wader counts rose sharply afterwards. Plants first, then the birds that feed on the flat, both tied to letting the tide back in.

whyWrong.B: The new inland wall is the engineering that made the breach possible and names no biological change.
whyWrong.C: The narrowing marsh describes the problem before the breach.
whyWrong.D: The 1850 wall is the original cause of the loss, not the change the question asks about.

tips: When a goal asks about the life of a site, the answer needs organisms in it, not just earthworks.
